entries.1:1: This introduces the book as Isaiah's message from God about Judah and Jerusalem, given during the reigns of four kings. It reminds the reader that God spoke through a real person at a real point in history.
entries.1:2: God calls heaven and earth as witnesses that he raised his people like children, yet they turned against him. It means God's care for us deserves loyalty, and turning away from him is a serious betrayal.
entries.1:3: Even farm animals know who feeds them, but God's people ignored him completely. The point for the reader is that ignoring the one who provides for you is worse than an animal's behavior.
entries.1:4: The people are described as deeply sinful and loaded with guilt because they abandoned the Lord. It warns the reader that rejecting God leads a whole life and community into corruption.
entries.1:5: God asks why they keep inviting more punishment instead of stopping. It means continuing in wrong ways only brings more pain, so it's time to stop.
entries.1:6: The nation is pictured as a body covered in untreated wounds from head to foot. It shows how sin leaves people battered and in need of healing, not more injury.
entries.1:7: Their land is ruined, towns burned, and crops taken by foreigners. The reader sees that turning from God can lead to real loss and devastation.
entries.1:8: Jerusalem is left like a lonely shelter in a field, surrounded by enemies. It pictures how vulnerable and abandoned a people become when God's protection is gone.
entries.1:9: If God had not spared a few survivors, the nation would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah. It reminds the reader that any survival and hope comes from God's mercy.
entries.1:10: God addresses the leaders and people as if they were Sodom and Gomorrah, urging them to listen to his teaching. It means religious status means nothing if you ignore God's word.
entries.1:11: God says their many sacrifices mean nothing to him because their hearts are wrong. It teaches the reader that going through religious motions without real obedience pleases no one.
entries.1:12: God asks who asked them to come trampling through his house with empty rituals. It means worship that ignores God's will is not welcome to him.
entries.1:13: God calls their offerings, festivals, and gatherings disgusting and tiresome because of their hypocrisy. The reader learns that religious activity without changed lives is offensive to God.
entries.1:14: God says their festivals have become a burden he is tired of carrying. It shows that even good practices become meaningless when done without sincerity.
entries.1:15: When they pray with hands stained by violence, God refuses to listen. It means God cares about how we treat others, not just how often we pray.
entries.1:16: God tells them to wash, clean up their lives, and stop doing evil. The reader is called to actually change behavior, not just feel sorry.
entries.1:17: They are told to do good, seek justice, and defend the fatherless and widows. It means real faith shows up in how we treat the vulnerable.
entries.1:18: God invites them to settle the matter together and promises that even deep, bloody sins can be made clean as snow. It means no one is too far gone for God's forgiveness.
entries.1:19: If they listen and obey, they will enjoy the good of the land. It means obedience leads to blessing and a good life.
entries.1:20: If they refuse and rebel, they will be destroyed by war. The reader is warned that rejecting God has serious consequences.
entries.1:21: The faithful city has become unfaithful, full of murder instead of justice. It shows how a community can drift from what is right and needs to be restored.
entries.1:22: Their silver is fake and their wine watered down. It means what looked valuable in their society had lost its true worth and integrity.
entries.1:23: Their leaders love bribes and ignore the fatherless and widows. The reader learns that corrupt leaders who neglect the vulnerable are condemned by God.
entries.1:24: God, the mighty Lord of Israel, declares he will deal with his enemies. It means God will not let injustice and opposition to him go on forever.
entries.1:25: God promises to purify his people like washing away dirt and removing fake metal. It means God's discipline is meant to clean and restore, not just punish.
entries.1:26: God will restore good judges and leaders, and the city will again be called righteous and faithful. It gives the reader hope that God can rebuild what has been ruined.
entries.1:27: Zion will be rescued and restored through justice and right living. It means God's salvation goes hand in hand with a changed, fair community.
entries.1:28: Sinners and those who abandon the Lord will be destroyed together. The reader is warned that turning away from God ends in ruin.
entries.1:29: They will be ashamed of the sacred trees and gardens they loved. It means trusting in things other than God eventually brings shame.
entries.1:30: They will be like a dried-up tree or a garden with no water. It pictures how life withers when it is cut off from God, the source of life.
entries.1:31: The strong and their works will burn like fuel in a fire no one can put out. It means human strength and achievement cannot save anyone who opposes God.
entries.2:1: This introduces a message God gave Isaiah about the future of Judah and Jerusalem. It reminds the reader that what follows is God's word, not just a man's opinion.
entries.2:2: In the days to come, God's mountain—where he dwells—will be raised above everything else, and people from every nation will stream toward it. It means God's rule will one day be the center of attention for the whole world.
entries.2:3: People will urge each other to go up to God's house so they can learn his ways and walk in his paths, because his teaching will go out from Jerusalem. It invites the reader to want to learn from God and to invite others along.
entries.2:4: God will settle disputes between nations, and weapons of war will be reshaped into farming tools; war will end. It means God's judgment brings real peace, and the reader can hope for a world without fighting.
entries.2:5: God's people are called to come and live in the light the Lord gives. It means the reader should choose to walk in God's ways rather than in darkness.
entries.2:6: God has set aside his people because they copied the occult practices of surrounding nations and made alliances with foreigners instead of trusting him. It warns the reader that adopting the world's ways in place of God has serious consequences.
entries.2:7: The land was full of silver, gold, horses, and chariots—signs of great wealth and military strength. It shows how easily abundance and power can become what a people rely on instead of God.
entries.2:8: The land was full of idols, and people worshiped things they had made with their own hands. It warns the reader against giving ultimate devotion to anything human-made.
entries.2:9: Both ordinary people and important people were brought low, and their sin would not be overlooked. It means no one, rich or poor, escapes the consequences of turning from God.
entries.2:10: People are told to hide in rocks and dust out of fear of the Lord's majesty and power. It pictures how small human pride becomes when faced with God's greatness.
entries.2:11: Human arrogance will be humbled and pride brought down, and the Lord alone will be exalted. It means God, not people, will finally be seen as supreme.
entries.2:12: A day is coming when the Lord will deal with all human pride and everything that exalts itself. It reminds the reader that no amount of self-importance will stand against God.
entries.2:13: The tall cedars of Lebanon and the strong oaks of Bashan—symbols of natural grandeur—will be brought down. It shows that even the most impressive things in creation are subject to God's judgment.
entries.2:14: Every high mountain and lifted-up hill will be brought low. It means the impressive, unshakable things people look up to will not escape God's humbling.
entries.2:15: Every tall tower and strong wall—human defenses and achievements—will be brought down. It warns the reader that human security systems cannot protect against God's judgment.
entries.2:16: Even the great trading ships and beautiful vessels will be brought low. It means commerce, luxury, and human glory are temporary and subject to God.
entries.2:17: Again, human pride will be humbled and the Lord alone lifted up. It reinforces that the final outcome is God's exaltation, not humanity's.
entries.2:18: The idols will completely disappear. It means the false gods people trusted in will be gone for good.
entries.2:19: People will hide in caves and holes in the ground out of fear when the Lord rises to shake the earth. It pictures the terror of facing God's power without humility.
entries.2:20: On that day people will throw away their silver and gold idols, giving them to animals in dark places. It means the things once treasured as gods will be discarded as worthless.
entries.2:21: People will hide in rocky crevices and caves out of fear of the Lord's glory when he shakes the earth. It shows that no hiding place can shelter anyone from God's majesty.
entries.2:22: Stop trusting in mere humans, whose life is only a breath and who cannot ultimately help. It tells the reader to put confidence in God rather than in fragile people.
entries.3:1: God is warning that he will soon remove everything the people of Jerusalem depend on to survive, starting with basic food and water. It means no amount of resources can protect you if God himself withdraws his support.
entries.3:2: God will also take away the people they rely on for leadership and skill, like soldiers, judges, prophets, and the wise. It means a society loses its stability when its capable people are removed.
entries.3:3: The same removal reaches every level of leadership, from military officers to advisers and those who practice magic. It means no human expert or official can hold a community together once God acts in judgment.
entries.3:4: God says he will let inexperienced and foolish people take charge. It means bad leadership is itself a form of judgment, and everyone suffers when the unqualified are in control.
entries.3:5: People will turn on each other, and respect for age and rank will break down. It means when society unravels, even ordinary relationships become harsh and chaotic.
entries.3:6: Things will be so bad that people will grab anyone with a coat and beg him to lead them. It means leadership will be desperate and based on nothing but appearances.
entries.3:7: The person will refuse, swearing he has nothing to offer and cannot help. It means in a collapsed society, no one wants the burden of responsibility because there is nothing left to give.
entries.3:8: Jerusalem and Judah are falling because their words and actions openly defy God and provoke him. It means persistent rebellion against God brings ruin on a whole community, not just individuals.
entries.3:9: Their shameless sin is as obvious as Sodom's was, and they no longer even try to hide it. It means when people stop being ashamed of wrongdoing, they are already heading toward disaster.
entries.3:10: God promises that those who do right will enjoy the good results of their choices. It means living uprightly is still worth it, even when everyone around you is falling apart.
entries.3:11: Those who do evil will personally suffer the consequences of their actions. It means sin is not free; the harm you cause comes back on you.
entries.3:12: The leaders of God's people are acting like children, and their guides are leading everyone off the right path. It means poor, immature leadership confuses people and sends them in the wrong direction.
entries.3:13: God himself is stepping forward to argue his case and judge his people. It means God does not ignore wrongdoing among those who belong to him; he holds them accountable.
entries.3:14: God will judge the elders and rulers for ruining his vineyard and keeping what they took from the poor in their own homes. It means leaders who exploit the vulnerable will answer to God for it.
entries.3:15: God demands to know why they crush his people and make life hard for the poor. It means God takes the mistreatment of the poor personally, as an attack on his own people.
entries.3:16: The women of Zion are proud, walking with haughty looks and flirting eyes, showing off their ankle chains. It means outward vanity and arrogance do not escape God's notice.
entries.3:17: God will bring disease on them and expose them to public shame. It means the beauty and status they trusted in will be stripped away.
entries.3:18: On that day God will remove all their fancy jewelry and ornaments. It means the things people use to display wealth and beauty will be taken from them.
entries.3:19: The list continues with earrings, chains, and fine clothing being taken away. It means every luxury they relied on for identity will be gone.
entries.3:20: Headbands, arm chains, perfume boxes, and lucky charms will all be removed. It means even their accessories and superstitions cannot save them.
entries.3:24: Instead of perfume there will be a bad smell, instead of a sash a rope, instead of styled hair baldness, and instead of fine clothes sackcloth and shame. It means pride and luxury will be replaced by humiliation and grief.
entries.3:25: Their men will fall by the sword and their soldiers will die in battle. It means the military strength they counted on will be destroyed.
entries.3:26: The city's gates will mourn and weep, and she will sit on the ground, empty and exposed. It means the proud city will end up humbled and deserted, like a grieving widow.
entries.4:1: So many men have died in war that women are desperate enough to beg one man to marry them, asking nothing but his name to remove their shame of being childless and alone. It shows how deeply sin and judgment have broken ordinary life.
entries.4:2: After that devastation, God promises new life will sprout and grow beautiful, and the land will produce good fruit for the survivors. It means God does not leave things broken forever; he brings fresh hope out of ruin.
entries.4:3: Those who survive in Jerusalem will be called holy and counted among the living, written down as belonging to God. It means God keeps a faithful remnant and marks them as his own.
entries.4:4: The Lord will wash away the filth and bloodguilt of his people through a tough, purifying judgment. It means God takes sin seriously and cleanses it thoroughly, not by ignoring it.
entries.4:5: God's presence will rest over every home and gathering in Zion like the cloud and fire that led Israel in the desert, covering them with his glory. It means God himself will be with and protect his people.
entries.4:6: That presence will give shade from the scorching heat and shelter from storm and rain. It means God offers real protection and relief to those who belong to him.
entries.5:1: God is pictured as a farmer singing a love song about his vineyard, which stands for his people. It shows how much care and affection he had for them.
entries.5:2: The farmer did everything a good vineyard owner could do, but the vines produced worthless grapes instead of good ones. God gave his people every advantage, yet they failed to live as he wanted.
entries.5:3: God invites the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge the situation for themselves. He wants them to see that the fault lies with them, not with him.
entries.5:4: God asks what more he could possibly have done for his people. When he looked for good fruit and found only bad, the disappointment was entirely on their side.
entries.5:5: Because the vineyard failed, the farmer will remove its protection and let it be trampled and ruined. God warns that he will withdraw his protection and let his people face the consequences.
entries.5:6: The vineyard will be left untended, overgrown with weeds, and deprived of rain. God is saying he will stop blessing and caring for a people who rejected him.
entries.5:7: The vineyard is explained: it is Israel and Judah, God's cherished people. He wanted justice and fairness, but found violence and cries of distress instead.
entries.5:8: A warning is given to greedy people who keep buying up houses and land until others have nowhere to live. God sees selfish accumulation and will not ignore it.
entries.5:9: God has revealed that many large, fine houses will end up empty and abandoned. Wealth built on greed does not last.
entries.5:10: Despite all the land and seed, the harvest will be tiny. God warns that greed and disobedience lead to loss rather than abundance.
entries.5:11: A warning is given to those who start drinking early and stay drunk late into the night. God sees people who chase pleasure and let it control their lives.
entries.5:12: At their parties they enjoy music and wine but pay no attention to what God is doing. It is a picture of people too distracted by pleasure to notice God at work.
entries.5:13: Because the people lacked understanding, they will be taken into exile, and even their leaders and partygoers will suffer hunger and thirst. Ignoring God leads to real loss.
entries.5:14: The grave opens wide to swallow up the crowds, their leaders, and their noisy celebrations. Death will take both the ordinary and the proud.
entries.5:15: Everyone, rich and poor alike, will be brought low and humbled. Human pride will be exposed and shamed.
entries.5:16: In contrast, God will be shown to be great and holy because he judges rightly. His justice is never compromised, even when people are proud.
entries.5:17: After the judgment, lambs and cattle will graze freely among the ruins. The land will be left to animals, showing how thoroughly it was emptied.
entries.5:18: A warning is given to those who drag their sin along like an animal on a rope, as if proud of it. They pull guilt closer instead of letting it go.
entries.5:19: These people mock God and demand that he hurry up and show his plans so they can see them. They treat God's warnings with scorn instead of taking them seriously.
entries.5:20: A warning is given to those who call evil good and good evil, who swap light for darkness and sweet for bitter. Twisting right and wrong is a serious offense to God.
entries.5:21: A warning is given to those who think they are wise and clever in their own eyes. Self-confidence can blind people to their real need for God.
entries.5:22: A warning is given to those who pride themselves on holding their drink and mixing strong drinks. Being proud of such things is foolish in God's eyes.
entries.5:23: A warning is given to those who take bribes to let guilty people go free and to deny justice to the innocent. God cares deeply about fair treatment for the innocent.
entries.5:24: Just as fire burns up stubble and dry grass, so these people will be destroyed at the root because they rejected God's law and word. Disobedience leads to ruin.
entries.5:25: God's anger burns against his people, and his judgment brings devastation and death. Even the hills shake, showing how serious his response to sin is.
entries.5:26: God will signal a distant nation to come quickly against his people. He can use even foreign powers to carry out his purposes.
entries.5:27: The invading army is described as tireless and fully ready, with no one exhausted or stumbling. Nothing will slow down the judgment that is coming.
entries.5:28: Their weapons are sharp and their horses and chariots fast like a storm. The enemy is well prepared and swift, leaving no room for escape.
entries.5:29: The attacking army roars like a lion and carries off its prey with no one able to rescue it. The people will be helpless against this force.
entries.5:30: On that day there will be roaring like the sea, and the land will be dark and full of trouble. Even the light will be swallowed by thick clouds, showing total distress.
entries.6:1: Isaiah saw a vision of the Lord sitting on a throne, exalted and majestic, with His robe filling the Temple. This shows God is the true King, even when an earthly king dies, and He remains sovereign over all.
entries.6:2: Winged heavenly beings stood above the Lord, using some wings to cover their faces and feet in reverence and others to fly. This pictures how even powerful heavenly creatures humbly honor God.
entries.6:3: The beings called out to one another that the Lord is perfectly holy and that His glory fills the whole earth. This reminds the reader that God's holiness and glory are not limited to one place but extend everywhere.
entries.6:4: The sound of the call shook the doorposts and filled the house with smoke. This shows the overwhelming power and awe-inspiring presence of God.
entries.6:5: Isaiah was overwhelmed with a sense of his own sin and ruin, especially his unclean speech, because he had seen the holy King. This teaches that encountering God's holiness makes us honest about our own sinfulness.
entries.6:6: One of the winged beings flew to Isaiah with a burning coal taken from the altar. This pictures God taking the initiative to deal with Isaiah's sin.
entries.6:7: The being touched Isaiah's mouth with the coal and declared that his guilt was removed and his sin atoned for. This shows that cleansing from sin comes from God's action, not our own effort.
entries.6:8: The Lord asked who would go on His behalf, and Isaiah immediately volunteered. This challenges the reader to be ready to answer God's call with willing obedience.
entries.6:9: God told Isaiah to go and speak to a people who would hear but not understand and see but not perceive. This warns that hearing God's word does not automatically produce understanding; hearts must be open.
entries.6:10: God described the people as becoming dull-hearted, hard of hearing, and blind so they would not turn to Him and be healed. This is a sober warning that persistent resistance to God can leave a person unable to respond.
entries.6:11: Isaiah asked how long this would last, and God answered until the land was left empty and ruined. This shows that God's judgment has a purpose and a limit, but it is real.
entries.6:12: The Lord would send the people far away, leaving the land desolate. This pictures the serious consequences of turning away from God.
entries.6:13: Even a small remnant left in the land would be burned again, yet like a stump left in the ground, a holy seed would remain. This gives hope that God preserves a remnant and brings new life from what seems destroyed.
entries.7:1: Two enemy kings marched against Jerusalem but could not defeat it. God was already protecting his people even before they trusted him.
entries.7:2: When Judah's king and people heard the enemy armies had joined forces, they panicked and shook with fear. Bad news can make anyone's heart tremble, but fear is not the same as the truth of what will happen.
entries.7:3: God sent Isaiah and his son to meet King Ahaz at a specific spot outside the city. God takes the first step to speak to a frightened king, and he brings a sign with him—the son's name means 'a remnant will return.'
entries.7:4: God told Ahaz to stay calm and not be afraid of these two enemy kings, who were like burnt-out sticks that only smoke. The threats that look terrifying may already be losing their power.
entries.7:5: Aram had plotted to harm Judah. The danger was real, not imagined.
entries.7:6: The plan was to invade Judah, terrify its people, and put a foreign king on the throne. Enemies wanted to wipe out God's chosen line of kings.
entries.7:7: God plainly said this plot would fail and never happen. What God declares will not stand, no matter how strong the plotters seem.
entries.7:8: Aram's power was only as big as its capital city and its king. God also said that within sixty-five years Israel would be shattered as a people. God knows the future and sets the limits on every nation.
entries.7:9: Israel's strength was only Samaria and its king. God gave Ahaz a simple choice: trust me and stand, or refuse and be broken. Faith is the difference between standing and falling.
entries.7:10: God spoke to Ahaz again through Isaiah. God kept reaching out even to a king who was already resisting him.
entries.7:11: God invited Ahaz to ask for any sign he wanted, from the deepest place to the highest heaven. God was willing to prove himself in a way Ahaz could not miss.
entries.7:12: Ahaz refused, pretending it would be wrong to test God. His words sounded religious, but they were really an excuse to avoid trusting God.
entries.7:13: Isaiah rebuked the royal family for wearing people out and now trying God's patience too. Refusing God's offer is not humility; it is another way of rejecting him.
entries.7:14: God himself would give a sign: a young woman would have a son and name him Immanuel, meaning 'God is with us.' God's promise of presence stands even when people refuse to ask for proof.
entries.7:15: The child would eat butter and honey, simple food of a poor or unsettled time, until he knew right from wrong. The sign would unfold over years, not overnight.
entries.7:16: Before that child grew old enough to choose good over evil, both enemy kings Ahaz feared would be gone and their land ruined. God's timing would prove true, and the threat would pass.
entries.7:17: God warned that trouble far worse than this would come on Ahaz, his people, and his family—the king of Assyria. Refusing God's help does not bring peace; it opens the door to greater trouble.
entries.7:18: God would whistle for Egypt and Assyria like a man calls his flies and bees. Even powerful nations move at God's signal.
entries.7:19: These armies would swarm everywhere—valleys, rocks, thorn bushes, and watering places. No corner of the land would escape the coming invasion.
entries.7:20: God would use Assyria like a hired razor to shave the king and people bare, a picture of total humiliation. The very nation Ahaz might trust for help would be the one that strips him.
entries.7:21: In that day a man would keep only one young cow and two sheep. Life would shrink to a small, simple survival.
entries.7:22: There would be so much milk that everyone left in the land could eat butter and honey. Even in judgment, God provides enough for those who remain.
entries.7:23: Vineyards once worth a thousand silver pieces would become nothing but briars and thorns. Wealth and careful work can be undone in a moment.
entries.7:24: People would carry bows and arrows just to go through the overgrown land. What was once farmland would become wild country where danger lurks.
entries.7:25: The hills once dug and planted would be left to roaming oxen and sheep because no one dared work them for fear of thorns. Fear of hardship can make people abandon good land and good work.
entries.8:1: God told Isaiah to write a name on a large board in ordinary letters so everyone could read it. The name was a sign of something about to happen, meant to be seen publicly.
entries.8:2: Isaiah was told to get respected witnesses to confirm the writing was genuine. This made the record official and trustworthy for later.
entries.8:3: Isaiah's wife became pregnant and had a son, and God told him to name the boy Maher-shalal-hash-baz. The child's name itself carried a message from God.
entries.8:4: Before the child could even say 'father' or 'mother,' Assyria would carry off the wealth of Damascus and Samaria. The timing shows how soon this would happen.
entries.8:5: God spoke to Isaiah again, adding more to what he had already said. This introduces the next part of his message.
entries.8:6: The people rejected God's gentle, quiet care and instead feared their enemies. Trusting the wrong thing led them away from the one who truly protected them.
entries.8:7: Because they rejected God's gentle care, he would let Assyria, like a mighty river, flood over them. The very power they feared would overwhelm them.
entries.8:8: The flood would sweep into Judah too, rising dangerously high, yet God's protection would still cover the land. Even in judgment, God's presence remained with his people.
entries.8:9: The nations are warned to take notice and be shaken. They may rage, but they are up against God.
entries.8:10: Whatever plans the nations make will fail, because God is with his people. Human schemes cannot stand against God's purpose.
entries.8:11: God warned Isaiah strongly not to follow the crowd's way of thinking. He was to stay loyal to God even when everyone else went another direction.
entries.8:12: Isaiah was told not to treat as sacred what the people treated as sacred, and not to share their fears. His fear was to be placed in God, not in what frightened the crowd.
entries.8:13: God himself is the one to be honored and feared above all. Giving him that place is what keeps a person steady.
entries.8:14: God would be a safe place for some but a stumbling stone for others in Israel. The same God who protects also confronts those who reject him.
entries.8:15: Many would stumble over that stone and be caught in the trap. Rejecting God's way leads to their own downfall.
entries.8:16: Isaiah was told to seal up his teaching and entrust it to his followers. God's message was to be preserved carefully for those who would receive it.
entries.8:17: Isaiah chose to wait patiently for God, even when God seemed hidden from his people. Waiting on God is an act of trust.
entries.8:18: Isaiah and his children were living signs from God to Israel. Their very lives pointed to what God was doing.
entries.8:19: People would urge others to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter. Isaiah asks whether it makes sense to seek the dead on behalf of the living instead of seeking God.
entries.8:20: The right response is to test everything against God's teaching and testimony. Those who reject it will find no light ahead of them.
entries.8:21: Such people will wander the land in hardship and hunger, and in their anger they will curse their king and their God. Their distress turns them against both human and divine authority.
entries.8:22: Looking around, they will see only trouble, darkness, and gloom. Rejecting God's light leaves a person in deep darkness.
entries.9:1: God first treated this northern region as unimportant, but later he will honor it—the same area by the sea and across the Jordan where Jesus would later minister. It means God can bring honor to places people overlook.
entries.9:2: People living in deep darkness and gloom will see a great light, meaning hope and rescue will come to them. For the reader, no situation is too dark for God to bring light into.
entries.9:3: God will give his people great joy, like the happiness of a good harvest or winning a battle. It reminds us that joy from God is deep and worth celebrating.
entries.9:4: God will break the heavy burden and cruel rod off his people's backs, just as he rescued them from Midian long ago. It means God is the one who frees people from oppression.
entries.9:5: Every soldier's boot and blood-stained uniform will be burned up, meaning war will finally end. It points to a future where fighting is over for good.
entries.9:6: A child will be born and a son given, and he will rule with titles like Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. This is a prophecy of Jesus, God's gift of a perfect ruler.
entries.9:7: His kingdom of justice and peace will never stop growing, established forever on David's throne. It means God's promise of a lasting, fair ruler is certain because God himself will do it.
entries.9:8: The Lord has sent a message of judgment that will fall on the northern kingdom of Israel. It shows God does not ignore his people's wrongdoing.
entries.9:9: All the people, especially Ephraim and Samaria, will feel this judgment—they are proud and confident in their own hearts. Pride keeps people from listening to God.
entries.9:10: In their pride they say they will rebuild better than before, replacing brick with stone and sycamores with cedars. It shows how people can defy God instead of humbling themselves.
entries.9:11: Because of their pride, God will strengthen Israel's enemies to attack them. It warns that refusing God invites trouble.
entries.9:12: Enemies from the east and west will attack Israel relentlessly, yet God's anger is still not finished. It shows that unrepentance brings ongoing consequences.
entries.9:13: Even after being punished, the people did not turn back to God or seek him. It reminds us that punishment is meant to bring us back to God, not just to hurt us.
entries.9:14: God will cut off both the leaders and the followers—the head and the tail—in a single day. It means no one escapes the results of turning away from God.
entries.9:15: The honored leaders are the head, and false prophets who teach lies are the tail. It warns against leaders who mislead people instead of guiding them toward truth.
entries.9:16: The leaders cause the people to wander off the right path, and both end up ruined. It shows how much damage bad leadership can do.
entries.9:17: God will show no pity even to the young, widows, and orphans, because everyone is godless and speaks foolishly. It is a serious warning that sin affects whole communities.
entries.9:18: Wickedness spreads like a fire burning through thorns and forests, sending up clouds of smoke. It pictures how sin grows and destroys everything in its path.
entries.9:19: The land is darkened by God's anger, and people turn on each other violently. It shows that when people reject God, society breaks down.
entries.9:20: People grab what they can on every side but are still hungry, and no one shows kindness to their own brother. It describes how selfishness and greed leave everyone empty.
entries.9:21: Even close tribes like Manasseh and Ephraim turn on each other and then attack Judah, yet God's anger continues. It warns that division and violence only make things worse.
entries.10:1: God pronounces judgment on leaders and lawmakers who use their power to make unjust rules. It means the reader should not use authority to harm others, because God sees and holds people accountable.
entries.10:2: These leaders deny justice to the poor and defenseless and take advantage of widows and orphans. It means God cares deeply about how the vulnerable are treated, so the reader should protect them rather than exploit them.
entries.10:3: God asks what these unjust leaders will do when punishment comes and help is far away. It means no amount of wealth or power will save anyone who has done wrong when God calls them to account.
entries.10:4: Even after all this, God's anger is not finished and his hand is still raised in judgment. It means God's justice is not partial or quickly exhausted; the reader should take his warnings seriously.
entries.10:5: God calls Assyria the rod of his anger, the tool he uses to carry out punishment. It means God can use even a powerful, violent nation to accomplish his purposes, though that nation is still responsible for its own actions.
entries.10:6: God sends Assyria against a people who have done wrong, to plunder them and crush them like dust. It means God's judgment is real, and the reader should not assume that wrongdoing will go unaddressed.
entries.10:7: Assyria, however, has its own plans—it wants to destroy and cut off many nations, not just to serve as God's tool. It means people and nations often pursue their own destructive ambitions even when God is using them for something else.
entries.10:8: The Assyrian king boasts that all his commanders are as good as kings. It means pride makes people overestimate themselves, and the reader should beware of the same arrogance.
entries.10:9: The king lists cities he has already conquered and asks whether the next ones will be any different. It means success can make people feel invincible, but that confidence is misplaced.
entries.10:10: He claims his hand has reached kingdoms with more idols than Jerusalem and Samaria had. It means he judges himself stronger than any god, which is dangerous pride before the true God.
entries.10:11: He says he will do to Jerusalem and its idols what he did to Samaria and its idols. It means he thinks Jerusalem's God is just another idol he can defeat, but he is badly mistaken.
entries.10:12: After God finishes his purpose against Jerusalem, he will punish the Assyrian king for his pride and arrogance. It means God holds even his instruments accountable, and no one's pride escapes his notice.
entries.10:13: The king boasts that he won everything by his own strength and wisdom. It means people often credit themselves for what God allows, and the reader should guard against that same self-congratulation.
entries.10:14: He brags that he took the wealth of nations as easily as picking up abandoned eggs, with no one resisting. It means his boast shows how blind he is to the God who actually gave him power.
entries.10:15: An axe cannot boast against the one who swings it, nor a rod against the one who lifts it. It means the Assyrian is only a tool, and the reader should remember that human power is always borrowed from God.
entries.10:16: Therefore the Lord will send wasting sickness and a burning fire into the Assyrian's strength. It means God can bring down the mightiest power from within, and no strength is safe from him.
entries.10:17: The God of Israel will be like a fire that burns up Assyria's thorns in a single day. It means God himself defends his people, and his judgment is swift and thorough.
entries.10:18: God will destroy Assyria's glory and its fields, body and soul together, like a wasting disease. It means the destruction will be complete, showing that no earthly splendor lasts when God acts against it.
entries.10:19: So few trees will be left that a child could count them. It means the once-mighty power will be reduced to almost nothing, and the reader should not envy or fear such temporary greatness.
entries.10:20: In that day the survivors of Israel will stop relying on the nation that oppressed them and will trust the Lord instead. It means hardship can turn people back to God, and the reader should put trust in him rather than in powerful allies.
entries.10:21: A remnant of Jacob will return to the mighty God. It means God preserves a faithful few even through judgment, and the reader can take hope that returning to God is always possible.
entries.10:22: Even though Israel's people are as numerous as sand, only a small number will return, because the destruction is firmly decided and just. It means numbers do not guarantee safety; what matters is faithfulness to God.
entries.10:23: The Lord of hosts is going to carry out this complete destruction throughout the land. It means God's declared judgment will certainly happen, so the reader should not treat his warnings as empty.
entries.10:24: God tells his people in Zion not to fear Assyria, even when its rod strikes them as Egypt once did. It means God's people may suffer for a time, but they need not be terrified of their oppressors.
entries.10:25: In a very short time God's anger against his people will end, and his wrath will turn against Assyria to destroy it. It means the suffering of God's people is temporary, while the oppressor's judgment is coming.
entries.10:26: The Lord will strike Assyria as he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb and as he struck Egypt. It means God has a track record of rescuing his people, and the reader can trust him to do it again.
entries.10:27: In that day the burden on Israel's back will be lifted and the yoke on their neck broken. It means God himself removes the weight of oppression, and the reader can look to him for freedom.
entries.10:28: The Assyrian army marches up through the towns, moving closer and closer to Jerusalem. It means the threat is real and near, and the reader should feel the tension of danger approaching.
entries.10:29: The army passes through the region, and nearby towns like Ramah and Gibeah are terrified and flee. It means fear spreads quickly when a powerful enemy comes, and no one is untouched by it.
entries.10:30: The towns are told to cry out and listen as the enemy draws near. It means the whole land is caught up in alarm, and the reader sees how far-reaching the threat has become.
entries.10:31: More towns flee or hide their belongings as the army advances. It means people are scrambling for safety, showing how helpless they are against such a force.
entries.10:32: That very day the enemy stops at Nob, just outside Jerusalem, and shakes his fist at the city. It means the danger is at the doorstep, and the reader feels how close the crisis has come.
entries.10:33: The Lord of hosts is about to cut down Assyria's branches with a great crash, bringing down its tall and mighty ones. It means God will suddenly and loudly bring down the proud, and the reader should not fear their height.
entries.10:34: God will cut down the thick forest with an axe, and even Lebanon's tall trees will fall. It means nothing is too big or too deeply rooted for God to bring down, so the reader should trust his power over all.
entries.11:1: A new leader will come from Jesse's family line, which looked cut down and finished, and this branch will bear good fruit. God can bring fresh hope and life out of something that seems dead or hopeless.
entries.11:2: God's Spirit will rest on this leader, giving him wisdom, understanding, good guidance, strength, and knowledge of God. This describes the kind of leader God provides, one guided by God himself.
entries.11:3: He will not judge by appearances or by what he merely hears. It reminds us that God's justice looks deeper than surface impressions.
entries.11:4: He will defend the poor and decide fairly for the needy, while his words will bring down the cruel and stop those who do evil. God cares about fairness for the vulnerable and holds the powerful accountable.
entries.11:5: Righteousness and faithfulness will be like the belt he wears, always with him. Good character is not occasional but part of who this leader is.
entries.11:6: Wild animals will live peacefully with gentle ones, and a small child will lead them. This pictures a world where fear and danger are gone and peace is real.
entries.11:7: Natural enemies like cows and bears will be at peace, and their young will rest together. It shows that old hostility and threat will be replaced by safety.
entries.11:8: Even a baby will play safely near a snake's hole, and a child will be safe near a poisonous snake. It pictures complete safety even where danger used to be.
entries.11:9: No one will be hurt or destroyed on God's holy mountain, because the whole earth will be filled with knowing the Lord. Knowing God will be as widespread and deep as water covering the sea.
entries.11:10: On that day the nations will look to this descendant of Jesse as a rallying sign, and his resting place will be glorious. People everywhere will be drawn to him and to the honor God gives him.
entries.11:11: On that day the Lord will reach out a second time to bring back the remaining people of his scattered nation from many distant lands. God does not forget his people, even when they are far away.
entries.11:12: He will raise a signal for the nations and gather the scattered people of Israel and Judah from every corner of the earth. God brings his scattered people back together.
entries.11:13: The jealousy between Ephraim and Judah will end, and their hostility toward each other will stop. Old family divisions and rivalries will be healed.
entries.11:14: Together they will stand against their enemies to the west and east and gain control over neighboring nations. Unity replaces division and gives them strength.
entries.11:15: The Lord will dry up the Egyptian sea and split the great river into seven streams so people can cross on dry ground. God removes impossible barriers so his people can come home.
entries.11:16: There will be a road for the remaining people coming back from Assyria, just as there was when Israel left Egypt. God makes a way home for his people, just as he did before.
entries.12:1: The speaker thanks God because his anger has passed and he has been comforted. It means you can thank God for forgiveness and for the relief that comes after hard times.
entries.12:2: God is the one who saves, so the speaker trusts him and refuses to be afraid. It means your strength and courage come from God, not from yourself.
entries.12:3: People will draw water from springs of salvation with joy. It means the rescue God gives is fresh and life-giving, and you can receive it gladly.
entries.12:4: People are told to thank God, honor his name, and tell other nations what he has done. It means your gratitude should be spoken out loud and shared with others.
entries.12:5: Sing to the Lord because he has done great things, and spread the news everywhere. It means God's good deeds deserve your praise and should be told to the whole world.
entries.12:6: The people of Zion are told to shout for joy because the great Holy One of Israel lives among them. It means you can celebrate, because God himself is near to his people.
entries.13:1: This verse introduces a message from God that Isaiah received about the city of Babylon. It reminds the reader that God speaks through his prophets and that proud nations are accountable to him.
entries.13:2: God tells the attacking armies to signal and shout so they can march against Babylon's leaders. It shows that God directs even the plans of foreign armies to carry out his purposes.
entries.13:3: God says he has called his warriors and ordered them to carry out his anger. The reader should understand that God is in control of history, even using powerful armies to judge evil.
entries.13:4: The sound of many nations gathering for battle is described, with the Lord himself organizing the army. It shows that a huge, organized force is coming because God has summoned it.
entries.13:5: These armies come from far away to bring destruction on the whole land as God's instruments. It means God's judgment is not limited to one place but is carried out by forces he directs.
entries.13:6: People are told to cry out because the day of the Lord is near, bringing destruction. It warns the reader that God's judgment is real and should be taken seriously.
entries.13:7: When that day comes, people's hands will go weak and their courage will melt away. It shows how terrifying God's judgment is, leaving even strong people helpless.
entries.13:8: People will be gripped by fear and pain like a woman giving birth, and they will look at each other in shock. It describes the panic and agony that come when God's judgment arrives.
entries.13:9: The day of the Lord is described as cruel and full of anger, making the land empty and destroying sinners. It reminds the reader that God's judgment against evil is severe and certain.
entries.13:10: The stars, sun, and moon will stop giving light, as if the whole sky is going dark. It shows that God's judgment is so great it affects the entire created order.
entries.13:11: God says he will punish the world for its evil, end pride, and bring down the cruel. It means no one who does evil, especially the proud, will escape God's justice.
entries.13:12: So few people will be left that a person will be harder to find than the finest gold. It shows how complete the destruction will be, leaving the land nearly empty.
entries.13:13: The heavens will shake and the earth will move from its place because of God's fierce anger. It pictures creation itself reacting to the power of God's judgment.
entries.13:14: People will run away like frightened deer or lost sheep, each hurrying back to his own people and land. It shows that when judgment falls, everyone scrambles to escape and find safety.
entries.13:15: Anyone caught will be killed with spears, and anyone who runs will be killed with swords. It describes the brutal reality of war that God's judgment brings on Babylon.
entries.13:16: Children will be violently killed before their parents' eyes, and homes and wives will be taken by others. It shows the terrible human cost of war and judgment, which should move the reader to sorrow over sin.
entries.13:17: God says he will stir up the Medes against Babylon, a people who care nothing for silver or gold. It means God can use any nation, even one not tempted by wealth, to carry out his plan.
entries.13:18: The Medes will be ruthless, killing young men and women and showing no pity to children. It shows how cruel the attacking army will be, fulfilling God's judgment on Babylon.
entries.13:19: Babylon, famous for its beauty and power, will be destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah. It reminds the reader that no city or empire, however glorious, can stand against God's judgment.
entries.13:20: No one will ever live in Babylon again, and even travelers and shepherds will avoid it. It shows that the destruction will be permanent, not just a temporary setback.
entries.13:21: Wild animals and jackals will live in the ruins, and people will say evil spirits dance there. It pictures a once-great city left as a haunted, empty wasteland.
entries.13:22: Wild animals will howl in the palaces and towers, and Babylon's time of power will end soon. It assures the reader that God's judgment will come quickly and the proud city will fall.
entries.14:1: God promises to show mercy to his people and bring them back home to their own land, and even foreigners will join them. This means God does not abandon his people forever, and outsiders are welcome to belong to his family.
entries.14:2: The nations that once held Israel captive will now help them and serve them, and Israel will rule over those who once ruled them. This means God can reverse a situation completely, turning captivity into freedom.
entries.14:3: This looks forward to the day God gives his people rest from their pain, trouble, and hard labor. It means relief from suffering is something God himself promises to bring.
entries.14:4: When that rest comes, the people will sing a mocking song about the king of Babylon, celebrating that his cruel rule has ended. It means proud, cruel leaders do not last forever.
entries.14:5: God himself has broken the power of the wicked and the authority of those who ruled harshly. It means God is the one who finally stops cruel rulers.
entries.14:6: This ruler had struck the peoples in endless anger and crushed nations without restraint. It means unchecked cruelty eventually brings its own judgment.
entries.14:7: Now the whole earth is calm and quiet, and people are singing for joy. It means when oppressive power falls, life and joy can return.
entries.14:8: Even the trees of Lebanon are glad, because no woodcutter comes against them anymore. It means all of creation feels relief when a destructive power is gone.
entries.14:9: The world of the dead stirs to meet this king when he arrives, and the kings already there rise from their seats. It means death humbles even the mightiest rulers.
entries.14:10: The dead kings ask him if he has become as weak as they are. It means no amount of power can keep a person from the same end as everyone else.
entries.14:11: His pride and his music have gone down to the grave, and worms cover him. It means earthly splendor and pride end in the dust.
entries.14:12: This describes the shining morning star falling from heaven down to the earth. It means even the most glorious and exalted figure can be brought low.
entries.14:13: This one said in his heart that he would climb to heaven and set his throne above God's stars. It means the root of his fall was wanting to be greater than God.
entries.14:14: He wanted to rise above the clouds and become like the Most High. It means pride that tries to take God's place always leads to downfall.
entries.14:15: Instead of rising, he is brought down to the deepest part of the grave. It means the higher pride climbs, the lower it falls.
entries.14:16: People stare at him in shock, asking if this is the one who shook the whole earth and troubled kingdoms. It means the world sees how empty great power becomes in the end.
entries.14:17: He had turned the world into a wasteland, destroyed towns, and never let his prisoners go free. It means a legacy of destruction and cruelty is remembered and judged.
entries.14:18: Other kings of the earth rest in honor, each in his own tomb. It means ordinary rulers at least receive a dignified burial.
entries.14:19: But this king is thrown out like a rejected corpse, covered with the slain and trampled underfoot. It means he loses even the honor of a proper burial.
entries.14:20: He will not rest with his ancestors, because he destroyed his land and killed his people, and his family line will be forgotten. It means evil done to others comes back on the one who did it.
entries.14:21: His children are to be put to death because of their father's evil, so they cannot rise up and fill the earth with ruin. It means the consequences of a leader's wickedness reach his family.
entries.14:22: God himself declares that he will cut off Babylon's name, descendants, and future generations. It means God will completely end this proud power.
entries.14:23: God will make Babylon a home for wild animals and a swamp, and sweep it away with destruction. It means the great city will become an empty ruin.
entries.14:24: God has sworn an oath that his plan will surely happen and his purpose will be carried out. It means God's word can be trusted completely.
entries.14:25: God will break Assyria in his own land and mountains, and remove the burden and rule it placed on his people. It means God himself will free his people from their oppressors.
entries.14:26: This is God's plan for the whole earth, and his hand is stretched out over all nations. It means no nation is outside God's authority.
entries.14:27: Since it is God's purpose, no one can cancel it, and no one can turn back his hand. It means God's plans cannot be stopped by human power.
entries.14:28: This message came to the prophet in the year King Ahaz died. It means God still speaks and acts at specific moments in history.
entries.14:29: Philistia should not celebrate that its oppressor is gone, because an even worse enemy will rise from that same line. It means rejoicing too soon over an enemy's fall can be a mistake.
entries.14:30: The poorest of God's people will be fed and kept safe, but Philistia's descendants will starve and its survivors will be killed. It means God cares for the poor while judging those who oppose him.
entries.14:31: The whole land of Philistia should cry out in grief, because an enemy is coming from the north like smoke, and no one will be left behind. It means judgment comes swiftly and no one can escape it.
entries.14:32: When foreign messengers ask, God's people can answer that the Lord founded Zion and it is a safe refuge for his poor people. It means God's city is a place of safety, especially for the weak and needy.
entries.15:1: This announces that the cities of Moab will be destroyed suddenly, overnight, so that nothing is left of them. It reminds the reader that no nation is safe from sudden ruin.
entries.15:2: The people of Moab go to their places of worship to weep, and they shave their heads and beards as a sign of grief. It shows how deeply they mourn when disaster strikes.
entries.15:3: People wear rough sackcloth and cry loudly in the streets, on their roofs, and in public squares. Their sorrow is open and everywhere, not hidden.
entries.15:4: The cries of grief spread from town to town, and the whole nation is shaken with fear. It pictures a people so frightened that their courage completely fails.
entries.15:5: God himself grieves over Moab as its people flee for their lives, weeping as they go. It shows that even in judgment, God is not cold or indifferent to human suffering.
entries.15:6: The streams dry up and all the grass and green plants die, leaving the land barren. It means the country loses the water and food it depends on.
entries.15:7: The people gather up whatever wealth and supplies they have saved and carry it away across the stream. It shows people trying to rescue what they can before everything is lost.
entries.15:8: The sound of weeping spreads all across Moab, from one border to the other. It means the grief and distress reach every part of the land.
entries.15:9: The waters of Dimon are filled with blood, and God says even worse is still coming, with danger waiting for those who try to escape. It warns that the suffering is not yet over.
entries.16:1: The people of Moab are told to send a gift to the ruler in Jerusalem as a sign of submission. It means the reader should see that help and safety come from God's chosen king, not from pride or self-reliance.
entries.16:2: The women of Moab are pictured as frightened birds that have lost their nest, scattered at the river crossings. It means people who lose their homes and security are desperate, and the reader should feel compassion for them.
entries.16:3: The people of Judah are asked to give shelter and wise advice to the fleeing Moabites, hiding them like the darkness of night. It means the reader is called to protect and help refugees instead of turning them away.
entries.16:4: Moab's outcasts are to be given a safe place to live among God's people until the cruel invaders are gone. It means the reader should offer lasting refuge to those who are oppressed, trusting that God will finally end the violence.
entries.16:5: A ruler from David's line will sit on a throne built on mercy, judging fairly and doing what is right without delay. It means the reader can hope in a just and kind king, which points to God's promised ruler.
entries.16:6: Moab is famous for its pride and loud boasts, but those boasts are empty and untrue. It means the reader should beware of arrogance, because proud claims do not match reality.
entries.16:7: Because of this, everyone in Moab will cry out in grief, mourning for the people of one of its towns. It means pride ends in sorrow, and the reader should take warning rather than gloat.
entries.16:8: The farmland and vineyards that made Moab rich are ruined, and the nations that traded with her are struck down. It means wealth and success can be wiped out quickly, so the reader should not build life on them.
entries.16:9: The prophet himself weeps for Moab's ruined vineyards and towns, even as war cries replace the harvest songs. It means God's people should grieve over the suffering of others, even their enemies.
entries.16:10: All the joy of harvest is gone, with no songs or shouts in the vineyards and no one treading grapes. It means when God's judgment comes, ordinary happiness disappears, and the reader should value joy as a gift.
entries.16:11: The prophet's heart aches and moans for Moab like a musical instrument played in grief. It means real sorrow for others is part of loving them, and the reader should let their heart feel for the suffering.
entries.16:12: When Moab prays at its shrines and temples, nothing happens and no help comes. It means false gods cannot save anyone, so the reader should put trust only in the living God.
entries.16:13: This is the message the Lord had already spoken about Moab in earlier times. It means God's warnings are not new or random, and the reader should take his words seriously.
entries.16:14: The Lord now says that within three years, counted like a hired worker's term, Moab's greatness will collapse and only a small, weak remnant will remain. It means God's timing is certain, and the reader should not assume proud nations or people will last.
entries.17:1: God announces that Damascus, a proud city, will be emptied and left in ruins. It reminds readers that no city or power stands forever when God has spoken against it.
entries.17:2: The towns around Damascus will be abandoned so completely that sheep will graze there undisturbed. What was once busy and populated becomes quiet pasture.
entries.17:3: The defenses of Ephraim and the rule of Damascus will both fall, and the remaining Arameans will lose their power and fade like Israel's former glory. God says that human strength and alliances cannot protect a nation from his judgment.
entries.17:4: In that day Israel's splendor will shrink and its strength will drain away. A people who trusted in their own greatness will be made small.
entries.17:5: It will be like a harvest where the grain is gathered up and nothing is left standing. The picture is of a complete stripping away, as when crops are cut in the valley of Rephaim.
entries.17:6: Still, a few will be left, like a handful of olives remaining after the tree is shaken. God's judgment is severe but not total; he preserves a small remnant.
entries.17:7: When that happens, people will finally look to the God who made them and turn their hearts to the Holy One of Israel. Hardship can bring people back to the One they should have trusted all along.
entries.17:8: They will stop trusting in the altars and idols their own hands made. The things people build to replace God will lose their hold on them.
entries.17:9: Israel's towns will become deserted like the ruins left by earlier peoples. The land that was once a gift and heritage will lie empty because of unfaithfulness.
entries.17:10: The people forgot the God who saved them and the Rock who gave them strength, and instead planted gardens for a foreign god. Forgetting God leads people to put their hope in things that cannot save.
entries.17:11: They tended their plants carefully and saw them sprout quickly, but the harvest will wither on a day of grief and pain. What looks promising at first can fail when God is left out.
entries.17:12: Many nations roar and rush in like crashing seas and floodwaters. The noise of human power is loud and frightening, but it is still only noise before God.
entries.17:13: God will stop them and scatter them like chaff blown off a mountain or dust caught in a storm. However great the threat, God can blow it away in a moment.
entries.17:14: By evening there is terror, and by morning the attackers are gone. This is what happens to those who plunder God's people: their violence comes back on them and ends in nothing.
entries.18:1: This announces a message about a distant land beyond Ethiopia's rivers, pictured as a place of buzzing wings. It means God is speaking about a far-off nation, showing that his reach extends to the whole world.
entries.18:2: This land sends messengers by sea in light boats to a tall, feared people whose land rivers divide. It means these envoys are told to hurry home, and it reminds the reader that even powerful nations are under God's notice.
entries.18:3: Everyone on earth is told to watch and listen when a signal flag is raised and a horn sounds. It means God is about to act in a way the whole world should pay attention to.
entries.18:4: God says he will stay quiet and watch from his place, like heat or dew settling on the land. It means God is not absent or asleep; he is calmly watching and waiting for the right moment.
entries.18:5: Before the grapes are ready to harvest, the spreading branches are cut back with knives. It means God steps in at just the right time to trim down pride and growth that has gone too far.
entries.18:6: The cut-off branches are left for birds and wild animals to feed on, in summer and winter. It means what was pruned away is left abandoned, a picture of total loss for what opposed God.
entries.18:7: At that time this tall, feared nation will bring an offering to the Lord at Mount Zion. It means even a powerful, distant people will end up honoring God, showing that he is Lord over all nations.
entries.19:1: God is pictured coming to Egypt like a rider on a fast cloud, and the nation's idols and courage collapse in fear. It means no country's gods or strength can stand when God shows up.
entries.19:2: God will cause Egypt to tear itself apart in civil conflict, with families, towns, and regions fighting each other. It means a nation that turns from God can destroy itself from within.
entries.19:3: Egypt's plans will fall apart, and the people will frantically turn to idols, mediums, and fortune-tellers for answers. It means when people reject God, they grasp at anything for guidance and find nothing solid.
entries.19:4: God will hand the Egyptians over to a harsh, cruel ruler. It means oppression is a real consequence of turning away from God, not something he ignores.
entries.19:5: The Nile and its waters will fail, drying up and leaving the land without its lifeline. It means Egypt's security, which depended on that river, can be taken away in a moment.
entries.19:6: The rivers will stink and shrink, and the reeds and plants along them will die. It means the whole system Egypt relied on for life and trade will break down.
entries.19:7: The fields and crops along the Nile will dry up or blow away and be gone. It means hard work and fertile land are worthless without God's blessing.
entries.19:8: The fishermen will grieve because there are no fish left to catch. It means ordinary workers suffer when a nation's foundations are judged.
entries.19:9: Those who make linen and cloth will be humiliated as their trade collapses. It means economic pride and skill cannot protect people from God's judgment.
entries.19:10: The workers who make thread will be crushed and deeply sad. It means the judgment reaches everyday laborers, not just the powerful.
entries.19:11: Egypt's wisest officials turn out to be fools, despite their proud claims of royal wisdom. It means human cleverness and pedigree mean nothing when God acts.
entries.19:12: The wise men are challenged to explain what God is doing, and they cannot. It means no human wisdom can predict or prevent God's plans.
entries.19:13: The leaders of Egypt's key cities have misled the nation and caused it to wander off course. It means bad leadership brings ruin on the people who follow it.
entries.19:14: God has confused Egypt's thinking so that its decisions stagger like a drunk man's steps. It means when God gives people over to confusion, even their best plans go wrong.
entries.19:15: No one in Egypt, from the highest to the lowest, will have anything useful to do. It means judgment reaches every level of society and leaves no one unaffected.
entries.19:16: The Egyptians will become weak with fear and tremble at God's power over them. It means facing God's power strips away all false confidence.
entries.19:17: Just hearing the name of Judah will terrify Egypt because of what God has planned. It means God's purposes make even powerful nations afraid.
entries.19:18: Five Egyptian towns will adopt the language of God's people and swear loyalty to the Lord. It means God's reach extends beyond Israel to bring outsiders to himself.
entries.19:19: An altar and a monument to the Lord will stand in the middle and at the edge of Egypt. It means worship of the true God will be established throughout that land.
entries.19:20: These will testify that when Egyptians cry out under cruel masters, God hears and sends them a rescuer. It means God responds to the cries of the oppressed, even outside his own people.
entries.19:21: The Egyptians will come to know the Lord and worship him with offerings and kept promises. It means knowing God changes how people live and worship.
entries.19:22: God will strike Egypt but then heal it, and when they turn back to him he will answer their prayers. It means God's discipline aims at restoration, not destruction.
entries.19:23: A road will connect Egypt and Assyria, and people from both former enemies will worship the Lord together. It means God can turn bitter enemies into a shared community of worship.
entries.19:24: Israel will join Egypt and Assyria as a third partner, and together they will be a blessing to the world. It means God's blessing is meant to flow through his people to all nations.
entries.19:25: God blesses Egypt as his people, Assyria as his handiwork, and Israel as his inheritance. It means God's love and purpose are wider than any one nation.
entries.20:1: This verse sets the historical scene: an Assyrian commander sent by King Sargon attacked and captured the city of Ashdod. It reminds the reader that these events really happened in a specific time and place.
entries.20:2: God told the prophet Isaiah to remove his outer clothing and sandals and walk around dressed like a captive. Isaiah obeyed, even though it made him look strange and shameful.
entries.20:3: God explained that Isaiah's odd appearance for three years was a living picture of what would happen to Egypt and Ethiopia. The reader learns that God sometimes uses visible signs to warn people of what is coming.
entries.20:4: Just as Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot, the king of Assyria would lead away the people of Egypt and Ethiopia as captives, stripped and humiliated. It shows that no nation's power can protect it from God's declared judgment.
entries.20:5: People who had trusted in Ethiopia and Egypt for help would be terrified and ashamed when those nations fell. It warns the reader not to put confidence in powerful allies who can fail.
entries.20:6: Those living along the coast would realize their hope in Egypt was useless against Assyria and ask who could possibly save them now. The point for the reader is that human help is fragile, and real security must come from somewhere greater.
entries.21:1: This is a message from God about a terrifying place of ruin, coming like a violent desert storm. It reminds the reader that God sees and announces judgment on proud nations before it happens.
entries.21:2: The prophet sees a frightening vision of betrayers and destroyers at work, and God calls the nations of Elam and Media to attack. It shows that God uses even violent nations to carry out his purposes.
entries.21:3: The prophet is so shaken by what he sees that he feels physical agony, like a woman in labor. It shows that God's coming judgment is serious and should move us, not leave us cold.
entries.21:4: His heart is confused and trembling, and the evening he looked forward to has turned into fear. It reminds the reader that sin and judgment turn hoped-for joy into dread.
entries.21:5: People are setting a table and feasting, but suddenly the call goes out to leaders to prepare for battle. It warns that people can be enjoying life right up to the moment danger strikes.
entries.21:6: God tells the prophet to station a watchman who will report whatever he sees. It shows that God warns his people ahead of time through faithful messengers.
entries.21:7: The watchman is told to pay close attention when he sees chariots, horsemen, and caravans of donkeys and camels. It teaches the reader to watch carefully for what God is doing in the world.
entries.21:8: The watchman cries out that he has stood at his post all day and all night. It pictures faithful, patient vigilance, the kind of watchfulness God's people are called to.
entries.21:9: The watchman sees riders coming and announces that Babylon has fallen and its idols are smashed. It declares that no proud power or false god can stand against God's judgment.
entries.21:10: The prophet speaks tenderly to his own crushed people, passing on the message God gave him. It shows that even words of judgment are meant to strengthen and steady God's people.
entries.21:11: A voice from Edom keeps asking the watchman how much of the night is left. It expresses the anxious longing of people waiting for relief from darkness and trouble.
entries.21:12: The watchman answers that morning is coming but night will return, and invites them to ask again. It tells the reader that hope is real but not yet complete, so keep seeking God.
entries.21:13: This message concerns Arabia, where traveling groups will have to spend the night in the scrubland. It shows that God's word reaches even distant peoples and their journeys.
entries.21:14: People of the land of Tema are told to bring water and bread to refugees on the run. It calls the reader to show practical kindness to people in desperate need.
entries.21:15: These refugees are fleeing from swords, bows, and the hardships of war. It reminds us that behind prophecies are real people suffering, and compassion is fitting.
entries.21:16: God says that within a year, all the splendor of Kedar will be gone. It shows that human wealth and glory are temporary and can end quickly by God's decree.
entries.21:17: Only a few of Kedar's archers and warriors will be left, because the Lord of Israel has spoken. It assures the reader that God's word is certain and will come true.
entries.22:1: This is a message about Jerusalem, called the valley of vision, and it asks why everyone has climbed onto their roofs. In that culture, rooftops were where people gathered in panic or celebration, so the question points to something dramatic happening.
entries.22:2: The city is noisy and celebrating, yet its people did not die in battle. Their joy is misplaced because disaster came another way, so the reader should not assume loud celebration means safety.
entries.22:3: The city's leaders and warriors ran away instead of defending the people. Those who should have protected others abandoned their posts, which is a warning about cowardly leadership.
entries.22:4: The prophet refuses comfort and weeps bitterly over the destruction of his people. He shows that real grief over suffering is right, even when the suffering was deserved.
entries.22:5: This is a day of panic, trampling, and collapse brought by the Lord of armies. It reminds the reader that God himself can bring judgment, not just distant human enemies.
entries.22:6: Foreign armies from Elam, Aram, and Kir are armed and ready for battle. The point is that the threat against Jerusalem is real and comes from many directions.
entries.22:7: The best valleys around Jerusalem are filled with chariots and horsemen lined up against the city. The reader sees that the enemy is close and the city is surrounded.
entries.22:8: Judah's defenses are stripped away, and the people start checking their weapons stored in the forest house. They turn to military preparation, which shows where their trust is going.
entries.22:9: They inspect the cracks in Jerusalem's walls and collect water in the lower pool. They are doing practical emergency work, but the text is building toward what they are not doing.
entries.22:10: They count the houses in Jerusalem and tear some down to repair the wall. This shows desperate effort to save the city by human planning alone.
entries.22:11: They build a reservoir for water but ignore the God who planned all this long ago. The reader is warned that practical fixes without looking to God miss the main point.
entries.22:12: On that day the Lord was calling for mourning, weeping, and signs of grief. God wanted repentance, not just repair work, and the reader should hear that call too.
entries.22:13: Instead of mourning, the people threw a party with meat and wine, saying they might as well enjoy life before they die. This is careless defiance, not honest faith, and it shows how easy it is to drown out God's call with pleasure.
entries.22:14: The Lord tells the prophet plainly that this sin will not be forgiven before death. It is a serious warning that refusing God's call can become permanent.
entries.22:15: God sends the prophet to confront Shebna, a high official who built himself an impressive tomb. The reader sees that self-important leaders can be called to account.
entries.22:16: Shebna is asked who he thinks he is and what right he has to carve out a resting place for himself there. His ambition is exposed as out of line.
entries.22:17: The Lord says he will grab this strong man and throw him away violently. Human power and status can be removed in an instant.
entries.22:18: Shebna will be rolled up like a ball and sent to a distant land, where he will die and his proud chariots will be a disgrace. His glory will end far from home.
entries.22:19: God will force Shebna out of his official position and pull him down from his place. No one should assume their job or rank is secure.
entries.22:20: God says he will call his servant Eliakim to take over. God himself chooses who will lead, replacing the proud with someone he calls his servant.
entries.22:21: Eliakim will be given Shebna's robe, sash, and authority, and he will care for Jerusalem and Judah like a father. Good leadership is described as protective and responsible.
entries.22:22: Eliakim will hold the key of David's household, and what he opens or shuts will stay that way. This means God gives real authority to the leader he appoints.
entries.22:23: God will set Eliakim firmly in place like a nail driven into a secure spot, and he will bring honor to his family. Stability and honor come from God's appointment, not self-promotion.
entries.22:24: The whole family's weight and glory will hang on him, down to the smallest cups and bowls. His position supports many people, so leadership carries responsibility for others.
entries.22:25: The Lord says even that firmly fixed nail will give way and be cut down, and everything hanging on it will fall. This warns that even a God-appointed position can be removed, so no one should put ultimate trust in human leaders.
entries.23:1: God announces that the great trading city of Tyre will be destroyed, so the ships that depended on it should mourn. It reminds the reader that no place is too strong or wealthy to escape God's judgment.
entries.23:2: The people along the coast and the merchants of Sidon, who grew rich through sea trade, are told to weep over the disaster. Those who profit from a fallen system share in its grief.
entries.23:3: Tyre's wealth came from grain shipped in from Egypt and from trade with many nations. Its prosperity rested on commerce, which God was about to bring down.
entries.23:4: The sea itself is pictured as grieving because it will no longer send out ships and sailors from Sidon. A proud port is left empty, like a mother with no children.
entries.23:5: When Egypt hears what happened to Tyre, its people will be deeply shaken because their own trade is tied to it. One nation's fall spreads fear and pain to others.
entries.23:6: The people of the coast are told to flee across the sea to Tarshish and mourn there. There is no safe place left for them to stay.
entries.23:7: This is the famous, ancient city that once celebrated and sent traders far across the world. The reader sees how quickly long-standing glory can end.
entries.23:8: The question is who planned Tyre's downfall, since its merchants were like princes and its businessmen were respected everywhere. Human importance does not protect a city from God's plans.
entries.23:9: The answer is that the Lord of hosts did it to humble human pride and bring down those the world honors. God opposes arrogance, however impressive it looks.
entries.23:10: Tarshish is told to turn its land back to farming because there is no longer a port to trade through. When trade collapses, people must find another way to live.
entries.23:11: God stretches out his hand over the sea and shakes kingdoms, giving orders to destroy Canaan's strongholds. No fortress can stand against his command.
entries.23:12: God says Sidon's joy is over, and even fleeing to Cyprus will bring no rest. Running away does not escape the consequences of judgment.
entries.23:13: This verse points to the Babylonians, a fierce people who built siege towers and turned a proud city into ruins. It reminds the reader that even the most powerful nations and defenses don't last forever.
