entries.23:14: The ships of Tarshish are called to wail because their safe harbor and trading base is ruined. Those who relied on Tyre's wealth now have nothing to return to.
entries.23:15: Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, roughly the length of one king's reign, and afterward it will start over like a prostitute singing to win back customers. God sets the time limit on a city's downfall.
entries.23:16: Tyre is pictured as a forgotten woman told to take up a harp, walk the streets, and sing catchy songs to be remembered again. It shows how it will work to attract business back.
entries.23:17: After seventy years God will let Tyre recover and resume trading with all the kingdoms of the world. God's mercy can restore even what he has judged.
entries.23:18: In the end Tyre's earnings will be dedicated to the Lord, not hoarded, and will supply food and clothing for those living in God's land. Wealth becomes right when it serves God's people instead of feeding pride.
entries.24:1: God is about to turn the whole earth into an empty ruin and scatter its people everywhere. It reminds the reader that no place on earth is beyond God's reach when he acts in judgment.
entries.24:2: When this judgment comes, it will not spare anyone based on rank or wealth—priests and servants, buyers and sellers, lenders and borrowers will all be treated the same. It means no social status can protect a person from God's reckoning.
entries.24:3: The land will be left completely empty and deserted because God himself has declared it. The reader should take God's word seriously, since what he says will certainly happen.
entries.24:4: The whole earth and world are mourning and fading, and even the most powerful people are brought low. It shows that human greatness offers no security when God brings ruin.
entries.24:5: The people have ruined the land by breaking God's laws, changing his rules, and violating the lasting covenant he made with them. It means our wrong choices have real consequences, not just for us but for the world around us.
entries.24:6: Because of this, the land falls under a curse and its people are judged as guilty, with fire consuming many and only a few left. The reader is warned that sin brings serious judgment, yet a remnant survives.
entries.24:7: The wine fails, the vines wither, and everyone who was happy now grieves. It pictures how judgment turns celebration into sorrow.
entries.24:8: The music of tambourines and harps stops, and the voices of happy people are silenced. It shows that joy without God does not last.
entries.24:9: People no longer sing as they drink wine, and strong drink tastes bitter to them. Even the simple pleasures people rely on are taken away in judgment.
entries.24:10: The city lies in ruins and every house is shut so no one can enter. It pictures total collapse and isolation when God's judgment falls.
entries.24:11: People cry out in the streets because the wine is gone, and all joy and gladness have disappeared from the land. It shows that when God removes his blessing, nothing can fill the emptiness.
entries.24:12: The city is left desolate and its public places are destroyed. The reader sees that what seemed strong and busy can become empty ruin.
entries.24:13: Among the peoples of the earth only a few will be left, like the few olives shaken from a tree or grapes left after harvest. It means judgment is severe, but God preserves a small remnant.
entries.24:14: Those who remain will lift their voices in joy and shout praise to the Lord from across the sea. Even in judgment, God's people have reason to worship him.
entries.24:15: People in the east and in distant coastal lands are called to give glory to the Lord, the God of Israel. It shows that God's praise is meant to reach every corner of the world.
entries.24:16: From the ends of the earth songs of praise go up to the righteous God, yet the prophet himself grieves because deceitful people keep on betraying and cheating. It reminds the reader that praise and sorrow can exist together while evil still runs its course.
entries.24:17: Terror, a pit, and a trap are coming upon everyone on earth. It means there will be no safe place to hide from God's judgment.
entries.24:18: Anyone who flees one danger will run into another—escape from terror leads to the pit, and escape from the pit leads to the trap—because the heavens open and the earth's foundations shake. It shows that running from God's judgment is futile.
entries.24:19: The earth is shattered, split apart, and violently shaken. It pictures creation itself breaking under the weight of God's judgment.
entries.24:20: The earth staggers like a drunk man and sways like a tent, crushed under the weight of its sin so it cannot rise again. It shows that sin is a burden too heavy for the world to carry.
entries.24:21: On that day God will punish both the powerful spiritual forces in the heavens and the kings of the earth. It means no power, visible or invisible, escapes God's judgment.
entries.24:22: They will be gathered together like prisoners locked in a dungeon, and after a long time they will be punished. It shows that judgment may be delayed, but it is certain.
entries.24:23: The moon will be ashamed and the sun disgraced because the Lord of hosts will reign in glory on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem before his elders. It means God's glory will outshine everything else when he finally rules openly.
entries.25:1: The speaker thanks God personally, praising him because the great things he planned long ago have actually come true. It invites the reader to trust that God keeps his promises and to thank him when they see it.
entries.25:2: God has brought down a proud, fortified city so completely that it can never be rebuilt. It reminds the reader that human power and pride do not last, but God's judgment is final.
entries.25:3: Because of what God has done, even powerful and cruel peoples will end up honoring him and fearing him. The reader can take comfort that God's power is greater than any bully or oppressive nation.
entries.25:4: God is like a shelter, a wall against storms, and shade from scorching heat for poor and hurting people. The reader who feels crushed can count on God as a safe place when trouble hits.
entries.25:5: Just as a cloud cools the heat, God silences the noise and boasting of cruel people. It means the loud threats of the powerful will be quieted, so the reader need not be afraid of them.
entries.25:6: On this mountain God will host a rich banquet of the best food and aged wine for every nation. It pictures God's future blessing and welcome for all peoples, giving the reader hope of joy to come.
entries.25:7: God will remove the dark covering and veil that hangs over all peoples. This means the confusion and grief that shadow humanity will be lifted, so the reader can look forward to clarity and comfort.
entries.25:8: God will destroy death forever and wipe away every tear, removing his people's disgrace everywhere. The reader can hope that grief and shame are not the end, because God himself promises to end them.
entries.25:9: On that day people will point to God and say he is the one they waited for and trusted, and they will celebrate. It encourages the reader to keep hoping, because waiting on God ends in joy.
entries.25:10: God's hand will rest on his mountain to bless it, while proud Moab will be trampled down like straw. It shows that God protects his people and brings down those who set themselves against him.
entries.25:11: Even if Moab spreads its hands like a swimmer trying to stay afloat, God will bring down its pride and clever schemes. The reader learns that no amount of skill or plotting can keep a proud person from God's judgment.
entries.25:12: God will tear down the high, strong walls of the proud city and flatten them into dust. It reassures the reader that no human defense is too strong for God to bring low.
entries.26:1: God's people will sing about how he protects them like a strong city with walls and towers. It means our safety comes from God, not from our own strength.
entries.26:2: The gates are opened so that a faithful, honest people can enter the city. It means God welcomes those who trust him and live rightly.
entries.26:3: God keeps steady, peaceful people whose minds are fixed on him, because they put their hope in him. It means trusting God brings real peace, even when life is hard.
entries.26:4: We should keep hoping in the Lord forever, because he is like a solid rock that never changes. It means God is reliable and worth trusting for the long haul.
entries.26:5: God brings down proud, arrogant people and their proud cities, leveling them to the ground. It means no human pride can stand against God.
entries.26:6: The poor and needy will trample the fallen proud city underfoot. It means those who were looked down on will see God's justice win.
entries.26:7: God makes the path of good and honest people straight and smooth. It means living rightly before God leads to a clear, steady way forward.
entries.26:8: God's people have waited for him and long to remember and honor his name. It means our deepest desire should be for God himself.
entries.26:9: The writer longs for God at night and seeks him early in the morning, because God's judgments teach the world what is right. It means wanting God more than anything, and learning from his correction.
entries.26:10: Even when God is kind, wicked people refuse to do right and keep on doing wrong instead of noticing God's greatness. It means kindness alone doesn't change a hard heart.
entries.26:11: God's hand is raised to act, but the wicked don't notice; they will finally see his judgment. It means ignoring God doesn't stop him from acting.
entries.26:12: God gives his people peace, and even their good works come from what he does in them. It means every good thing we accomplish is really God's work.
entries.26:13: Other rulers have ruled over God's people, but they now trust only in the Lord for salvation. It means we should look to God alone to save us.
entries.26:14: Those dead rulers won't rise again; God has destroyed them and wiped out their memory. It means God's enemies are finished for good.
entries.26:15: God has made the nation great and expanded its borders. It means God is the one who brings growth and honor to his people.
entries.26:16: When trouble came, God's people turned to him and prayed under his discipline. It means hard times can push us to pray.
entries.26:17: The people cried out in pain like a woman in labor. It means their suffering was intense and real.
entries.26:18: They went through pain but produced nothing lasting—no rescue, no new life came from their efforts. It means human effort alone can't save the world.
entries.26:19: God promises that the dead will rise and those in the dust will wake and sing. It means death is not the end for God's people; he will bring them back to life.
entries.26:20: God tells his people to hide safely behind closed doors for a short time until his anger passes. It means God protects his people while judgment runs its course.
entries.26:21: The Lord is coming to punish the earth's people for their evil, and the earth will no longer hide the blood that was shed. It means God will bring every hidden wrong to light and settle the score.
entries.27:1: God is pictured as a warrior who will finally defeat the great sea monster that stands for everything evil and chaotic. For the reader, it means God will one day put an end to the powers of evil that seem so strong now.
entries.27:2: God's people are compared to a lovely vineyard, and a song is sung about it. It means God sees his people as something beautiful and worth celebrating.
entries.27:3: God says he personally watches over his vineyard and waters it constantly, day and night, so nothing harms it. For the reader, it means God is actively protecting and caring for his people at all times.
entries.27:4: God says his anger is over, but if thorns and weeds of rebellion fight against him, he will burn them up. It means God is no longer against his people, but he still opposes what would destroy them.
entries.27:5: The only other option is for anyone to surrender to God and make peace with him. It means the safe path for the reader is to stop resisting God and accept peace with him.
entries.27:6: In the future Israel will take root, bud, and blossom, and the whole world will be filled with its fruit. It means God's people will grow strong again and bless the world around them.
entries.27:7: God asks whether he has punished his people as harshly as he punished their enemies. The implied answer is no, meaning God's discipline of his own people is not like the destruction he brings on their foes.
entries.27:8: God describes how he dealt with his people by driving them away with a strong wind, like a measured punishment rather than total destruction. It means even God's hard discipline is measured and has a purpose.
entries.27:9: The people's sin is forgiven when they tear down their altars and idols and stop worshiping them. It means real forgiveness shows itself in getting rid of the things that pulled you away from God.
entries.27:10: The strong city is left empty and ruined, with animals grazing where people once lived. It means pride and power without God end up as a wasteland.
entries.27:11: The dried branches are broken off and burned because the people are foolish and ignore their Maker. It means refusing to listen to God leads to ruin, and there comes a point when he lets people face the results.
entries.27:12: God will carefully gather his scattered people back home, from one end of the land to the other, like a farmer gathering grain. It means God does not forget his people, even when they are scattered, and he brings them back with care.
entries.27:13: A great trumpet will sound, and those who were scattered to Assyria and Egypt will come home to worship God in Jerusalem. It means God will bring his wandering people back to himself, and they will worship him together.
entries.28:1: God warns the proud, drunken leaders of Ephraim that their glory is already fading like a dead flower. Pride and excess don't protect you; they mark you for a fall.
entries.28:2: God will send a powerful enemy that sweeps in like a flood and storm and overwhelms them. No amount of self-confidence can stop it.
entries.28:3: The proud, drunken leaders will be trampled down. What they boast in will be crushed, not honored.
entries.28:4: Their fading splendor will be snatched away quickly, like someone eating the first ripe fruit the moment they see it. Their glory won't last.
entries.28:5: In that day God himself will be the true glory and beauty for the faithful remnant of his people. Real honor comes from him, not from pride.
entries.28:6: God will give judges the wisdom to rule fairly and soldiers the strength to defend the city gates. He supplies what his people truly need.
entries.28:7: Even priests and prophets are staggering from drink, so their visions are false and their judgments unreliable. When leaders are drunk on wine, they lead people astray.
entries.28:8: Their tables are filthy with vomit, leaving no clean spot anywhere. Drunkenness makes a mess of everything it touches.
entries.28:9: The prophet asks who will listen to God's teaching, implying the people act like babies who only understand the simplest things. They refuse to grow up in understanding.
entries.28:10: God's word comes to them in tiny, repetitive bits, like teaching a child one rule and one line at a time. They can only handle the most basic instruction.
entries.28:11: Since they won't listen to clear teaching, God will speak to them through foreign invaders with a strange language. Judgment itself becomes the message.
entries.28:12: God offered them rest and refreshment for the weary, but they refused to listen. The peace he offered was rejected.
entries.28:13: So God's word will become for them a stumbling block of endless rules, and they will fall backward, be broken, and be trapped. Rejecting God's rest leads to ruin.
entries.28:14: The prophet now addresses the proud rulers of Jerusalem directly. They especially need to hear God's warning.
entries.28:15: They claim a deal with death will protect them from disaster, trusting lies instead of God. False security is still false, no matter how confident it sounds.
entries.28:16: God is laying a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion, and whoever trusts in it will not be shaken. Faith in God's foundation is the only real security.
entries.28:17: God will measure with justice and righteousness, and the storm will wash away every refuge built on lies. What is false cannot stand when God judges.
entries.28:18: Their deal with death will be canceled, and the flood they thought would pass them by will overwhelm them. Trusting in lies leaves you exposed.
entries.28:19: The disaster will come again and again, morning after morning, day and night, until the news alone terrifies them. There will be no escape from the recurring judgment.
entries.28:20: The bed is too short and the blanket too small to cover them. Their false comforts cannot actually protect or satisfy them.
entries.28:21: God will rise up to act as he did in past battles, but his work will seem strange and shocking to them. God's judgment is real, even when it surprises us.
entries.28:22: Stop mocking God, or your chains will only get tighter, because a complete destruction has been decreed for the whole land. Scoffing at warning only makes things worse.
entries.28:23: The prophet calls the people to listen carefully to what he is about to say. Paying attention to God's word is the first step toward wisdom.
entries.28:24: A farmer doesn't plow forever; he prepares the soil and then stops to plant. God's discipline also has a purpose and a limit.
entries.28:25: Once the ground is ready, the farmer plants different seeds in their proper places. God knows exactly what to do and when, just as a skilled farmer does.
entries.28:26: The farmer learns these methods because God teaches him. God gives practical wisdom to those who work the land.
entries.28:27: Delicate spices are beaten gently with a stick, not crushed with heavy wheels. God deals with each thing according to what it needs.
entries.28:28: Bread grain is not crushed endlessly; the farmer knows when to stop. God's judgment is measured and purposeful, not endless destruction.
entries.28:29: All this wisdom comes from the Lord of armies, who plans wonderful things and is wise in everything he does. God's ways are skillful and purposeful, even when we don't fully see it.
entries.29:1: God calls Jerusalem by the name Ariel and warns that even though the people keep celebrating their yearly festivals, trouble is coming. Going through religious routines means nothing if God is about to act against the city.
entries.29:2: God says he himself will bring distress on Jerusalem, and the city will be full of mourning and crying. The point is that God is the one behind the coming judgment, not a random enemy.
entries.29:3: God will surround Jerusalem like an army laying siege, cutting it off and building towers against it. The city that felt safe will find itself trapped.
entries.29:4: Jerusalem will be brought down low, its voice coming faint and muffled from the ground like a ghost whispering. Defeat will leave the city humbled and weak.
entries.29:5: The enemies attacking Jerusalem will vanish like dust or dry chaff blown away by wind, and it will happen suddenly. The threat that looks huge will disappear in a moment.
entries.29:6: God himself will come with thunder, earthquake, storm, and fire to rescue his people. He is not a distant observer but a powerful defender who acts on their behalf.
entries.29:7: All the nations attacking Jerusalem will end up like a dream that fades when you wake. Their seeming victory will turn out to be nothing real.
entries.29:8: The attackers will be like a hungry or thirsty person who dreams of eating and drinking but wakes up still empty. Their hopes of conquering Jerusalem will leave them with nothing.
entries.29:9: The people are told to be stunned and blind, staggering as if drunk even though they have had no wine. Their own spiritual confusion will leave them unable to see what is happening.
entries.29:10: God has put the people into a deep spiritual sleep, and even the prophets and seers can no longer see. When people ignore God, even their ability to understand him can be taken away.
entries.29:11: God's message to them is like a sealed book that even a literate person cannot read because it is closed. The words are there, but the people cannot get at their meaning.
entries.29:12: The message is also like a book handed to someone who cannot read, who says he doesn't know how. Either way, the people are unable to understand what God is saying.
entries.29:13: The people say the right words and honor God with their lips, but their hearts are far from him, and their worship is just human rules learned by rote. God cares about the heart, not just outward religious performance.
entries.29:14: Because of this, God will do something astonishing that confounds the people, and the wisdom of their wise leaders will prove useless. Human cleverness cannot substitute for genuine devotion to God.
entries.29:15: Woe to those who try to hide their plans from God and think no one sees what they do in the dark. Nothing is actually hidden from God, no matter how secret people think they are.
entries.29:16: It is upside down to think the clay can tell the potter what to do or deny that it was made. We are the created, not the creator, and we have no right to tell God he doesn't understand.
entries.29:17: In a very short time the whole landscape will be transformed, with barren Lebanon becoming fertile and fertile land becoming forest. God can completely reverse the situation people expect.
entries.29:18: On that day people who could not hear will hear the words of the book, and the blind will see through the darkness. God will open ears and eyes that were closed.
entries.29:19: The poor and needy will find fresh joy in the Lord and rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. God lifts up the lowly and gives them a reason to celebrate.
entries.29:20: The cruel will be gone, those who mocked God will disappear, and those plotting evil will be cut off. God will remove the people who cause harm and scoff at him.
entries.29:21: These are the ones who use false testimony to trap people, set snares for honest judges, and rob the innocent of justice. God sees those who pervert justice and will deal with them.
entries.29:22: The Lord, who rescued Abraham, says that Jacob's family will no longer be ashamed or afraid. God's saving character toward his people has not changed.
entries.29:23: When Jacob's descendants see what God has done among them, they will honor his name and stand in awe of the Holy One of Jacob. Seeing God's work produces genuine reverence.
entries.29:24: Those who had wandered from God will gain understanding, and those who complained against him will listen to his teaching. God can turn confused and rebellious hearts back toward learning from him.
entries.30:1: God calls his people stubborn children because they make their own plans and alliances without asking him, which only adds to their sin. It warns us that going our own way instead of seeking God's guidance only makes things worse.
entries.30:2: They were going down to Egypt to get military help without asking God first, trusting Pharaoh's power instead of him. It means we can be tempted to lean on powerful people or resources rather than on God.
entries.30:3: The very strength they hoped would save them will end up embarrassing them, and their hope in Egypt will fail. Whatever we trust instead of God will eventually let us down.
entries.30:4: Their officials had already arrived in Egyptian cities to negotiate the deal. It shows how far they went to arrange help from a source God had not approved.
entries.30:5: The help they sought from Egypt will bring them nothing but shame and disgrace because Egypt cannot actually help them. It reminds us that help from the wrong source leaves us worse off.
entries.30:6: This describes a dangerous journey south through wild, hostile land carrying riches to a nation that gives no benefit in return. It pictures how costly and pointless it is to chase help that cannot deliver.
entries.30:7: Egypt's help is useless, and God calls her a loud, boastful power that has come to nothing. It means we should not be impressed by things that make big claims but cannot actually save.
entries.30:8: God tells Isaiah to write this message down permanently so future generations can see it and learn from it. It shows that God's warnings are meant to be remembered, not forgotten.
entries.30:9: The people are rebellious and dishonest, refusing to listen to what the Lord teaches. It warns us about the danger of hardening our hearts against God's instruction.
entries.30:10: They tell the prophets to stop telling them the truth and instead say things that please them. It's a picture of people who only want messages that make them comfortable, not honest ones.
entries.30:11: They want the prophets to get off the right path and stop bringing God before their minds. It shows how people try to push God out of their thinking so they can live as they please.
entries.30:12: Because they reject God's word and trust in deceit and oppression instead, God announces judgment. It means rejecting the truth and relying on lies will not go unpunished.
entries.30:13: Their sin is like a crack in a high wall that suddenly gives way and collapses. It warns that hidden problems from sin can bring sudden, unexpected ruin.
entries.30:14: God will smash them like a clay pot broken so completely that no useful piece is left. It shows that the consequences of persistent sin can be total and beyond repair.
entries.30:15: God said their salvation came through quiet trust and rest in him, but they refused. It means real strength is found in calmly trusting God rather than in frantic self-reliance.
entries.30:16: They insisted on fleeing on fast horses, so God says they will indeed flee, and their enemies will be faster. It shows that proud self-confidence often brings the very thing we fear.
entries.30:17: Their enemies will terrify them so badly that a thousand will run from one, leaving them isolated like a lone flag on a hill. It pictures how completely fear and defeat can scatter a people who trust in themselves.
entries.30:18: Even so, the Lord waits to show them kindness and mercy, and he blesses everyone who hopes in him. It means God is patient and ready to restore those who turn back to him.
entries.30:19: God promises that the weeping of his people in Jerusalem will end, and he will answer them when they cry. It means God hears our cries and will bring comfort in his time.
entries.30:20: Even when God allows hard times, he promises his people will no longer ignore their teacher but will see him clearly. It means hardship can teach us to pay attention to God again.
entries.30:21: God promises a voice behind them guiding them to turn the right way when they are unsure. It means God actively guides those who are willing to listen.
entries.30:22: They will throw away their silver and gold idols as something filthy and say good riddance to them. It means true repentance means getting rid of the things we have put in God's place.
entries.30:23: God promises rain for their crops and plenty of good food, with cattle grazing in wide pastures. It shows that when God restores his people, he provides abundantly for their needs.
entries.30:24: Even the working animals will have good, clean feed. It's a picture of such complete abundance that every need, great and small, is cared for.
entries.30:25: Streams of water will flow on every high mountain and hill in the day of great victory when enemy towers fall. It pictures God bringing life and refreshment even in places that were dry and hopeless.
entries.30:26: The moon and sun will shine far brighter than before when the Lord heals his people's wounds. It means God's restoration will be so complete it's like a whole new level of light and life.
entries.30:27: The Lord's name comes from far away, burning with anger and thick smoke, ready to act against evil. It reminds us that God takes sin seriously and will not ignore it forever.
entries.30:28: His breath is like a flood that rises to the neck, shaking nations and leading them astray to their ruin. It pictures God's power overwhelming those who oppose him.
entries.30:29: God's people will sing like they do on a holy festival night, joyful as they go up to worship the Lord. It means God's deliverance brings deep joy and worship, not just relief.
entries.30:30: The Lord will make his voice heard and show his power with fire, storm, and hail. It shows that God's judgment is real and powerful, not something to take lightly.
entries.30:31: The Assyrian enemy will be broken by the voice of the Lord, and his own rod of punishment will be turned against him. It means God himself defends his people against those who oppress them.
entries.30:32: Every blow God strikes against the enemy will be accompanied by music, and he will wage war against him. It pictures God's victory over evil as something that brings joy to his people.
entries.30:33: A place of burning has long been prepared, deep and wide, and the breath of the Lord sets it ablaze. It's a picture of final judgment prepared for the proud king who opposed God.
entries.31:1: God warns against trusting in powerful nations and military strength, like Egypt's horses and chariots, instead of trusting him. It means relying on anything other than God for safety leads to trouble.
entries.31:2: God is wise and will not let evil go unpunished, and he will act against those who do wrong and against whatever they trusted for help. It means no one can outsmart God or escape his justice by leaning on other powers.
entries.31:3: Egypt's help is only human and weak, not divine, so when God acts, both the helper and the one being helped will fall together. It means human allies cannot save you when God himself is against the situation.
entries.31:4: Just as a lion is not scared off from its prey by shouting shepherds, God will not be deterred from defending Mount Zion. It means God's commitment to protect his people is fearless and unstoppable.
entries.31:5: God will hover over Jerusalem like birds protecting their young, shielding and rescuing it from danger. It means God personally guards and saves those he protects.
entries.31:6: The people had deeply sinned against God, and he calls them to turn back to him. It means no matter how far you have wandered, God invites you to return.
entries.31:7: A day is coming when people will throw away the silver and gold idols they made for themselves. It means the things we wrongly trust will eventually be abandoned when we see they are worthless.
entries.31:8: Assyria will be destroyed by a sword that is not a human one, meaning God himself will defeat them, and their young men will be forced into labor. It means God can bring down a powerful enemy without any human army.
entries.31:9: Assyria's stronghold will collapse in panic and its leaders will flee in fear, because the Lord, whose fire and altar are in Zion, is the one acting. It means God's presence with his people is what brings down their enemies.
entries.32:1: A good king will rule fairly and honestly, and his officials will make just decisions. This means leaders should be trustworthy and fair to the people they lead.
entries.32:2: This good ruler will protect people like a shelter from wind and storms and like cool water and shade in a hot, dry land. For the reader, it means good leadership gives safety and relief when life is hard.
entries.32:3: People will see clearly and listen carefully to what is said. It means the time will come when people understand the truth instead of being blind and deaf to it.
entries.32:4: People who act rashly will learn to think wisely, and those who struggle to speak will be able to speak clearly. This gives hope that people can grow and change for the better.
entries.32:5: Foolish and dishonest people will no longer be treated as important or honorable. It means people will stop giving respect to those who do not deserve it.
entries.32:6: A foolish person says foolish things and plans evil, even speaking falsely about God and refusing food and water to those who need them. It warns that foolishness shows itself in how people treat the needy.
entries.32:7: Dishonest people plan to ruin the poor with lies, even when the poor are in the right. This reminds the reader that God sees unfair treatment of the poor and it is not ignored.
entries.32:8: A person with a noble heart makes noble plans and stands by them. It encourages the reader to let good character guide their choices.
entries.32:9: The prophet calls out to women who live at ease and feel safe to listen carefully. It warns that comfort and confidence can make people careless about what is coming.
entries.32:10: In about a year, these carefree people will be troubled because the grape harvest will fail. It means hard times are coming, so false security will not last.
entries.32:11: Those who feel safe are told to tremble, be troubled, and put on clothes of mourning. It means they should wake up to their danger and grieve instead of ignoring it.
entries.32:12: The people are told to mourn for the fields, the pleasant land, and the fruitful vines. It shows that the coming judgment will bring real loss to the land they enjoyed.
entries.32:13: Thorns will grow over the land of God's people, even in the happy houses and the joyful city. It means the places of joy will become wild and neglected.
entries.32:14: Fine houses will stand empty and the noisy city will become deserted, with the hill and watchtower left empty for wild animals. It pictures total ruin where life and activity once were.
entries.32:15: This ruin will last until God's Spirit is poured out from above, turning the wasteland into a fertile field and the fertile field into a forest. It gives hope that God himself can bring new life out of devastation.
entries.32:16: Then justice will live even in the wilderness, and righteousness will be at home in the fertile field. It means God's fair and right way of living will spread everywhere.
entries.32:17: Righteousness will produce peace, and its result will be lasting safety with no fear. For the reader, doing what is right leads to calm and security rather than anxiety.
entries.32:18: God's people will live in peaceful homes, free from fear, in quiet places of rest. It promises that God's people can look forward to safety and calm.
entries.32:19: But the forest will fall with a great crash and the city will be brought low. It reminds the reader that pride and human strength will be humbled.
entries.32:20: Those who plant seed beside every water and let their ox and donkey roam freely will be happy. It pictures blessing and plenty for people who work and live in God's good land.
entries.33:1: This warns a destroyer who has been attacking people who never harmed him that his own destruction is coming. It means cruel people who take advantage of others will eventually face the same treatment themselves.
entries.33:2: This is a prayer asking God for mercy and help because the people have been waiting on him. It means we can ask God to be our strength each morning and our rescue when trouble comes.
entries.33:3: When God acts with power, whole nations scatter in panic. It means no people or army can stand against God when he rises to defend his cause.
entries.33:4: The wealth left behind by defeated enemies gets gathered up quickly, like swarms of locusts stripping a field. It means the plunder of the wicked ends up taken by others just as fast as it was gained.
entries.33:5: God is exalted and lives in the highest place, and he fills his city with justice and right living. It means God's greatness is shown in the fairness and goodness he brings to his people.
entries.33:6: God's people will be secure, saved, wise, and full of knowledge, and reverence for God will be their true treasure. It means trusting and honoring God gives a stability and wealth that circumstances cannot take away.
entries.33:7: The warriors cry out in the streets and the messengers of peace weep bitterly because peace has failed. It means when negotiations break down, even the strongest and most hopeful are left grieving.
entries.33:8: The roads are empty and travel has stopped because the treaty was broken and the enemy shows no respect for people. It means broken promises and cruelty leave a land isolated and unsafe.
entries.33:9: The whole land mourns and withers, and even lush regions like Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan, and Carmel are drying up. It means the damage of war and sin spreads to the land itself, not just to people.
entries.33:10: God declares that now is the time for him to act, to rise up and show his power. It means when things seem hopeless, God steps in at his chosen moment to make his strength known.
entries.33:11: The plans of the wicked produce nothing lasting and are consumed by God's fiery breath. It means schemes built on evil collapse and cannot survive God's judgment.
entries.33:12: The nations will be burned up like lime or like cut thorns thrown into fire. It means powerful enemies are as fragile as dry brush when God acts against them.
entries.33:13: God calls both those far away and those nearby to pay attention and recognize what he has done. It means everyone, near or far, is invited to see and acknowledge God's power.
entries.33:14: Sinners in the city are terrified and ask who can survive God's consuming fire. It means guilt makes people afraid of God's holiness, and no one can stand before him on their own.
entries.33:15: This describes the person who can dwell with God: one who is honest, refuses bribes and violence, and turns away from evil. It means God honors those who live with integrity and refuse to profit from wrongdoing.
entries.33:16: Such a person will be kept safe in a high, rocky refuge with reliable food and water. It means living rightly brings God's protection and provision even in hard times.
entries.33:17: The people will see their king in his splendor and look out over a wide, open land. It means God's people will enjoy the beauty and security of good leadership and freedom.
entries.33:18: The people will look back on their former fears and wonder where the enemy officials and record-keepers went. It means the threats and burdens that once terrified you will fade into memory.
entries.33:19: The arrogant, foreign-speaking oppressors will no longer be seen. It means the intimidating power of cruel enemies will be gone for good.
entries.33:20: Jerusalem will be a peaceful, secure home like a tent that is never moved or torn down. It means God's people will finally have lasting rest and safety.
entries.33:21: God himself will be present with his people in glory, with broad rivers and streams where no enemy ships can sail. It means God's presence is our protection, and no threat can reach us there.
entries.33:22: The Lord is described as judge, lawgiver, king, and savior all in one. It means God himself takes full responsibility for leading, ruling, and rescuing his people.
entries.33:23: The enemy's rigging hangs loose and their sails cannot catch wind, so even the blind and lame will share the plunder. It means God defeats the strong so completely that the weakest win the spoils.
entries.33:24: No one in Zion will say they are sick, because the people's sin has been forgiven. It means God's forgiveness brings healing and wholeness, removing the sickness that sin caused.
entries.34:1: God is telling every nation and every person on earth to stop and listen carefully, because what he is about to say concerns everyone. The reader should pay attention too, since God's words are not just for ancient people but for the whole world.
entries.34:2: God is deeply angry with the nations and their armies because of their evil, and he has decided to destroy them completely. This reminds the reader that God does not ignore cruelty and injustice forever.
entries.34:3: The dead will be so many that they lie everywhere and the ground is soaked with blood. It is a picture of total defeat, showing how serious God's judgment is.
entries.34:4: The sky itself will wear out and roll up like a scroll, and the stars will fall away like dead leaves. Even the heavens are not permanent compared to God's power.
entries.34:5: God's judgment, pictured as a sword, is ready in heaven and is about to fall on Edom, a nation he has marked for punishment. The reader learns that no nation escapes God's justice.
entries.34:6: The image shifts to a great slaughter, like animals killed for a feast, because God is judging the people of Edom. It shows that God's anger is real and his judgment is thorough.
entries.34:7: Even the strongest among them will fall along with the weak. No amount of strength or status will protect anyone from God's judgment.
entries.34:8: This is the day God settles the score for the wrongs done to his people. The reader can trust that God sees injustice done to his people and will answer it in his time.
entries.34:9: The land's rivers will turn to burning tar and its dust to fire, so the whole place becomes a blazing wasteland. It shows complete ruin, not just a setback.
entries.34:10: The fire will never go out and the smoke will rise forever, and no one will ever pass through that land again. The destruction is permanent, a warning of how final God's judgment can be.
entries.34:11: Only desert birds and scavengers will live there, and the land will be marked out as empty and worthless. What was once inhabited becomes a home only for wild creatures.
entries.34:12: The leaders and rulers will be gone, and people will say that kingdom no longer exists. Human power and government can be wiped out when God decides.
entries.34:13: Thorns and weeds will grow in the fine houses and strong towers, and wild animals will live in the ruins. What people built with pride becomes a home for foxes and owls.
entries.34:14: Wild creatures and eerie night spirits will meet in the ruins and cry out to each other. The place becomes so deserted that it feels haunted and frightening.
entries.34:15: Snakes will nest and hatch their eggs there, and hawks will gather in pairs. Even the animals settle in, showing the land is now theirs and not people's.
entries.34:16: God tells the reader to check his book, because everything he promised will happen exactly as written, with nothing missing. God's word is reliable, and he makes sure it all comes true.
entries.34:17: God himself has assigned this land to those wild creatures and measured it out for them to keep forever. Even in judgment, God's plan is orderly and sure, and what he decides stands for all time.
entries.35:1: Even land that is empty and dry will come alive and be glad, bursting with flowers. It means God can bring life and joy to places that seem hopeless, including your own dry seasons.
entries.35:2: The land will bloom richly and everyone will sing for joy as God's greatness is seen. It means God's power shows up in visible, joyful change that people can actually see.
entries.35:3: Strengthen people whose hands are weak and whose knees are shaky. It means encourage those who are worn out or losing hope instead of leaving them to struggle alone.
entries.35:4: Tell frightened people to be brave because God is coming to rescue them and make things right. It means fear does not get the last word, since God himself comes to save.
entries.35:5: People who could not see will see and people who could not hear will hear. It means God fixes what is broken in us, so no disability or limitation is beyond his help.
entries.35:6: People who could not walk will jump for joy and people who could not speak will sing, because water bursts out in the desert. It means God's rescue brings such relief that even the impossible becomes a reason to celebrate.
entries.35:7: Hot sand will turn into pools of water and dry ground into springs, so even grazing land becomes green and wet. It means God turns the most barren situations into places where life can grow.
entries.35:8: There will be a road called the Holy Way, and God's people will walk it safely without losing their way. It means God gives a clear, safe path forward for those who belong to him.
entries.35:9: No lion or dangerous animal will be on that road, and it is kept for those God has rescued. It means God protects his people on the journey, so they need not fear being harmed along the way.
entries.35:10: Those God sets free will come home singing, with lasting joy, and sorrow and grief will be gone forever. It means God's rescue ends in joy that never runs out, and your sadness will not last forever.
entries.36:1: Assyria's powerful king attacked and captured all of Judah's fortified cities. It shows how serious the threat was and sets up the crisis that follows.
entries.36:2: The Assyrian king sent a high official with a large army to confront Jerusalem directly. The city was now face to face with a powerful enemy.
entries.36:3: Three of King Hezekiah's top officials went out to meet the Assyrian representative. They were sent to hear what the enemy had to say.
entries.36:4: The Assyrian official challenged Hezekiah directly, asking what he was really trusting in. It's a taunt meant to shake their confidence.
entries.36:5: He dismissed their battle plans as empty talk and demanded to know who would actually help them. He was trying to make them feel helpless.
entries.36:6: He warned that relying on Egypt was like leaning on a cracked stick that would pierce the hand. It's a vivid picture of a support that fails and hurts you.
entries.36:7: He tried to twist their faith, arguing that Hezekiah had insulted God by removing shrines. He was using half-truths to undermine their trust in God.
entries.36:8: He mocked them with a bet: he'd give them horses if they could even find riders. The point was that they were hopelessly outmatched.
entries.36:9: He sneered that they couldn't even handle the weakest of his master's officers. He wanted them to feel small and defeated before the fight began.
entries.36:10: He claimed God had actually sent Assyria to destroy the land. This was a bold and false claim designed to confuse and frighten them.
entries.36:11: The Judean officials asked him to speak in a foreign language so the people on the wall wouldn't understand. They wanted to keep the frightening words from spreading panic.
entries.36:12: He refused, saying his message was meant for the ordinary people who would suffer in a siege. He deliberately aimed his threats at everyone, not just the leaders.
entries.36:13: He then shouted loudly in the people's own language so everyone could hear. He wanted the whole city to hear the king of Assyria's message.
entries.36:14: He warned the people not to let Hezekiah fool them, claiming he couldn't save them. It was a direct attack on their king's leadership.
entries.36:15: He told them not to trust Hezekiah's promise that God would protect the city. He was trying to separate the people from their leader and their faith.
entries.36:16: He offered them a deal: surrender and live peacefully, each enjoying their own vine, fig tree, and water. It sounded attractive but meant giving up their freedom.
entries.36:17: He promised to move them to a land just as good as theirs, with grain, wine, bread, and gardens. It was a tempting offer meant to make surrender seem safe.
entries.36:18: He argued that no other nation's gods had saved them from Assyria, so their God wouldn't either. He was trying to make God seem powerless.
entries.36:19: He listed cities whose gods had failed to protect them. His point was that Jerusalem's God would be no different.
entries.36:20: He challenged them to name even one god that had stopped him, implying the Lord couldn't either. It was a direct insult to God's power.
entries.36:21: The people stayed silent because the king had ordered them not to respond. Their silence was obedience, not agreement with the taunts.
entries.36:22: The officials returned to Hezekiah with torn clothes, a sign of deep distress, and reported everything. The situation was grave, and the king needed to know how bad it was.
entries.37:1: When Hezekiah heard the enemy's threats, he was deeply upset, so he tore his clothes and put on rough sackcloth as a sign of grief. He then went straight to God's house, showing that turning to God is the right first response when we are afraid.
entries.37:2: Hezekiah sent his top officials and leading priests, also wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. This shows he wanted God's word on the matter and treated it as serious enough to involve the nation's spiritual leaders.
entries.37:3: Hezekiah described the situation as a time of deep trouble and disgrace, using the picture of a woman in labor with no strength to deliver. It means the crisis was real and they felt completely helpless to fix it themselves.
entries.37:4: Hezekiah hoped God had heard the enemy's insults against the living God and would act on them, and he asked Isaiah to pray for the remaining people. It shows that when we are powerless, prayer is still something we can do.
entries.37:5: The officials simply delivered Hezekiah's message to Isaiah. This is a plain transition showing the request for prayer was actually carried out.
entries.37:6: God told Hezekiah through Isaiah not to be afraid of the insulting words the Assyrian king's men had spoken against him. It means God takes personally the mockery aimed at his people and tells them not to panic.
entries.37:7: God promised to put a certain spirit in the Assyrian king so that a rumor would send him home, where he would be killed. It means God can turn a powerful enemy around using something as small as a piece of news.
entries.37:8: The Assyrian spokesman found his king had left Lachish and was attacking Libnah instead. This shows the enemy's plans were already shifting, just as God had said.
entries.37:9: When the Assyrian king heard that Tirhakah of Ethiopia was coming to attack him, he sent another message to Hezekiah. It means the enemy was now under pressure from another direction but still tried to intimidate Judah.
entries.37:10: The message warned Hezekiah not to let his God give him false hope that Jerusalem would be spared. It was a direct attack on his trust in God, trying to make him doubt what God had promised.
entries.37:11: The king reminded Hezekiah of how Assyria had destroyed every other land and asked how he could possibly escape. It is the classic bully tactic of using past victories to create fear.
entries.37:12: He listed nations whose gods failed to save them from his ancestors. The point was that no god had ever stopped Assyria, so Judah's God would be no different in his eyes.
entries.37:13: He named more defeated kings and towns to drive home the same point. It piles on examples to make the threat feel overwhelming and certain.
entries.37:14: Hezekiah took the letter, read it, then went up to the Lord's house and spread it out before God. It is a picture of bringing our fears and threats honestly and openly to God in prayer.
entries.37:15: This simply introduces the prayer Hezekiah then prayed to the Lord. It marks the moment he turns from the letter to talking with God.
entries.37:16: Hezekiah began by praising God as the commander of heavenly armies, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, and the only God and maker of heaven and earth. Starting with who God is helps put the problem in proper perspective.
entries.37:17: He asked God to listen and see and to take notice of all the insulting words Sennacherib had sent against the living God. It means he wanted God to see the injustice and act on it.
entries.37:18: Hezekiah honestly admitted that Assyria really had destroyed many nations and their lands. He was not in denial about the enemy's power; he was bringing the facts to God.
entries.37:19: He pointed out that those nations' gods were only wood and stone made by human hands, so of course they were destroyed. The real issue was not Assyria's strength but that they had mocked the living God.
entries.37:20: He asked God to save them so that every kingdom on earth would know that the Lord alone is God. His request was not just for safety but for God's name to be honored.
entries.37:21: God answered through Isaiah, telling Hezekiah that his prayer against Sennacherib had been heard. It shows that God listens and responds when his people pray.
entries.37:22: God's word says that Jerusalem, pictured as a young woman, will laugh at the Assyrian king instead of being afraid of him. It means the one who threatened God's people will end up humiliated.
entries.37:23: God asks the king whom he thought he was insulting, and the answer is the Holy One of Israel himself. It means the boasts against Judah were really boasts against God.
entries.37:24: The king had bragged through his servants about conquering mountains, cutting down Lebanon's cedars, and reaching the highest places. It shows his arrogance and his belief that nothing could stop him.
entries.37:25: He boasted of digging wells and drying up Egypt's rivers with his own feet. It is more swaggering talk about his power over water and land.
entries.37:26: God answers that he had planned all this long ago and now simply let it happen, so that the king was only a tool in turning strong cities into ruins. It means Assyria's success was not really its own doing.
entries.37:27: That is why the people of those cities had no strength and were crushed, like grass in a field or on a roof that withers in the wind. It explains their weakness as God's doing, not Assyria's greatness.
entries.37:28: God says he knows everything about the king, from when he sits down and gets up to all his comings and goings. It means no one is hidden from God, however powerful they are.
entries.37:29: Because of the king's rage and pride against God, God says he will put a hook in his nose and a cord in his lips and send him back the way he came. It means God will firmly control and turn back this proud enemy.
entries.37:30: God gave a sign: for two years the people would eat what grew by itself, and in the third year they would plant and harvest and plant vineyards. It was a promise that normal life and food supply would return.
entries.37:31: The survivors of Judah would take root again and bear fruit. It means the nation would not be wiped out but would recover and grow again.
entries.37:32: A remnant would come out of Jerusalem and Mount Zion, and God's determined purpose would make it happen. It means the survival of God's people was guaranteed by God's own plan, not by their strength.
entries.37:33: God declared that the Assyrian king would not enter the city, shoot an arrow at it, come at it with shields, or build a siege ramp against it. It is a clear promise of complete protection.
entries.37:34: He would go back the same way he came and never get into the city. It means the threat would end without the enemy ever setting foot inside Jerusalem.
entries.37:35: God said he would defend the city for his own honor and for the sake of his servant David. It means God's protection rested on his own name and his promises, not on Judah's worthiness.
entries.37:36: The angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 men in the Assyrian army, and in the morning there were only dead bodies. It shows God himself defeated the enemy without Judah fighting a battle.
entries.37:37: Sennacherib, the Assyrian king, withdrew and went back home to Nineveh. It means the threat was truly over and the enemy retreated as God had promised.
entries.37:38: While Sennacherib was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his own sons killed him with swords and fled, and another son took the throne. It shows that the proud king met his end exactly as God had said, in his own place of worship.
entries.38:1: God sends Isaiah to tell King Hezekiah he is going to die, so he should get his affairs in order. It reminds the reader that death can come unexpectedly and we should be ready.
entries.38:2: Hezekiah turns away to face the wall and prays to God in private. It shows that turning to God in prayer is the natural response when we are afraid or facing death.
entries.38:3: Hezekiah asks God to remember how faithfully and wholeheartedly he has lived, and then he cries bitterly. It shows honest grief and the desire to be remembered by God for a life lived well.
entries.38:4: God responds to Hezekiah's prayer by speaking to Isaiah again. It shows that God hears and answers when people pray.
entries.38:5: God tells Hezekiah that he has heard his prayer and seen his tears, and promises him fifteen more years of life. It shows that God is moved by our prayers and tears and can grant more time.
entries.38:6: God also promises to protect Hezekiah and Jerusalem from the Assyrian king. It shows that God's care covers both the person and the community.
entries.38:7: Isaiah tells Hezekiah that God will give him a visible sign to confirm the promise. It shows God graciously gives reassurance that his word is true.
entries.38:8: God makes the shadow on the stairway go backward ten steps as a sign. It shows God can reverse the normal order of things to confirm his promise.
entries.38:9: This introduces a written record by Hezekiah after he recovered from his illness. It shows that remembering and writing down what God has done is valuable.
entries.38:10: Hezekiah recalls thinking that in the middle of his life he would go down to the place of the dead and lose his remaining years. It expresses the fear of dying too soon.
entries.38:11: He thought he would never again see the Lord or other people in this world. It shows how death felt like being cut off from worship and from life with others.
entries.38:12: He describes his life being pulled down like a tent and cut off like thread from a loom, with pain from day to night. It pictures how quickly and painfully life can be taken away.
entries.38:13: He cries out in pain all night, feeling as if his bones are being crushed like a lion would. It shows the intense physical and emotional suffering of his illness.
entries.38:14: He compares his cries to a bird and a dove, looking upward for help, and asks God to rescue him. It shows that even in deep distress he turns his eyes to God.
entries.38:15: He wonders what he can say, since God himself has done this, and he cannot rest at night. It shows the struggle of accepting hardship that comes from God's hand.
entries.38:16: He waits on the Lord, asking for restored strength and healing so he can live again. It shows hope and dependence on God for recovery.
entries.38:17: He says his soul was full of bitterness instead of peace, but God rescued him from death and forgave his sins. It shows that God's rescue includes both physical healing and forgiveness.
entries.38:18: He notes that the dead cannot praise God or hope in his mercy. It reflects the belief that praising God is something the living do.
entries.38:19: The living person praises God, as Hezekiah does, and parents pass on the story of God's faithfulness to their children. It shows that telling the next generation about God's mercy matters.
entries.38:20: He asks the Lord to save him quickly, so that they can make music and sing in the Lord's house all their lives. It shows gratitude expressed through worship.
entries.38:21: Isaiah gives a practical instruction to put a cake of figs on the sore spot so Hezekiah will recover. It shows that God's healing can come through simple, ordinary means.
entries.38:22: Hezekiah asks what sign will show that he will go up to the Lord's house. It shows the desire for confirmation that he will worship God again.
entries.39:1: The king of Babylon sent messengers with a gift to Hezekiah after hearing he had been sick and recovered. It looked like a friendly gesture, but it set up a test of Hezekiah's heart.
entries.39:2: Hezekiah was pleased to see them and showed off everything he owned, holding nothing back. His pride led him to display his wealth to people he should have been cautious with.
entries.39:3: The prophet Isaiah came and asked Hezekiah what the visitors had said and where they were from. Hezekiah answered that they had come from far away, from Babylon.
entries.39:4: Isaiah pressed him on what the visitors had seen, and Hezekiah admitted he had shown them everything. He could not deny that he had held nothing back.
entries.39:5: Isaiah then told Hezekiah to listen carefully, because God had a message for him. The prophet was about to deliver a serious word from the Lord.
entries.39:6: God said that a time was coming when all the wealth in Hezekiah's house and all his ancestors had stored up would be carried off to Babylon. Nothing would be left.
entries.39:7: Even some of Hezekiah's own sons would be taken away and made servants in the palace of the king of Babylon. The judgment would touch his own family.
entries.39:8: Hezekiah accepted God's word as good, and he was relieved that there would be peace and quiet during his own lifetime. He seemed more concerned about his own comfort than about what would happen later.
entries.40:1: God tells his people to be comforted and reassured. For the reader, it means God cares about your pain and wants you to receive comfort, not just give it.
entries.40:2: God says Jerusalem's hard time of punishment is over and she has paid more than enough. For the reader, it means guilt and suffering do not last forever with God; he speaks tenderly when the hardship ends.
entries.40:3: A voice calls out to clear a straight road through the desert for the Lord to come. For the reader, it means get ready, because God is about to show up in your life.
entries.40:4: Every low place will be raised and every high place flattened so the road is smooth. For the reader, it means God removes the obstacles that stand between him and his people.
entries.40:5: God's greatness will be seen openly by everyone, and God himself has promised it. For the reader, it means God's glory is not hidden forever; it will be visible to all.
entries.40:6: A voice says to shout, and the answer is that people are as short-lived as grass and wildflowers. For the reader, it means human strength and beauty fade quickly, so don't build your life on them.
entries.40:7: Grass dries up and flowers die when God's breath blows over them, and people are just like that. For the reader, it means our lives are fragile and depend on God's breath every moment.
entries.40:8: Grass dries and flowers die, but God's word stands forever. For the reader, it means when everything else fails, God's promises remain reliable.
entries.40:9: The messenger of good news should shout boldly from a high place, without fear, that God is here. For the reader, it means share God's good news confidently and don't be afraid.
entries.40:10: The Lord comes with power and brings his reward and rescued people with him. For the reader, it means God is strong and will not forget to bring his people home.
entries.40:11: Like a shepherd, God feeds his flock, gathers the lambs in his arms, and gently leads the nursing ewes. For the reader, it means God is tender and careful with the weak and vulnerable among his people.
entries.40:12: No one can measure the oceans, span the heavens, weigh the earth's dust, or balance the mountains; only God can. For the reader, it means God is far greater than anything we can measure or control.
entries.40:13: No one has directed the Lord's Spirit or taught him anything. For the reader, it means God doesn't need our advice; he already knows everything.
entries.40:14: No one gave God counsel, taught him the right path, or instructed him in wisdom. For the reader, it means God's wisdom is his own and never depends on human input.
entries.40:15: To God, whole nations are like a drop in a bucket or dust on a scale, and islands weigh like fine dust. For the reader, it means no human power is impressive compared to God.
entries.40:16: Even Lebanon's forests and all its animals would not be enough for a proper sacrifice to God. For the reader, it means no offering we could give is ever enough to match God's greatness.
entries.40:17: All nations count as nothing before God, less than nothing and worthless. For the reader, it means don't be impressed or intimidated by earthly powers; God is above them all.
entries.40:18: God asks who could possibly be compared to him. For the reader, it means nothing in this world is a fair comparison to God, so don't reduce him to something smaller.
entries.40:19: A craftsman carves an idol and a goldsmith covers it with gold and adds silver chains. For the reader, it means idols are just human-made objects, not gods.
entries.40:20: A poor person picks a wood that won't rot and hires a skilled worker to set up an idol that won't fall over. For the reader, it means even the best-made idol is still just a thing that needs to be propped up.
entries.40:21: God asks if they haven't known or heard this from the beginning, since the earth was founded. For the reader, it means the truth about God has been obvious all along; we have no excuse for ignoring it.
entries.40:22: God sits above the circle of the earth, stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and people look like grasshoppers to him. For the reader, it means God is vastly greater than us and sees the whole picture.
entries.40:23: God brings rulers to nothing and makes the earth's judges worthless. For the reader, it means human authorities rise and fall, but God remains in charge.
entries.40:24: Rulers barely get planted and take root before God blows on them and they wither and the storm carries them off. For the reader, it means powerful people can be gone in a moment; don't rely on them.
entries.40:25: The Holy One asks who could be considered his equal. For the reader, it means God alone is holy and supreme; nothing compares to him.
entries.40:26: Look up at the stars: God created them all, calls each by name, and keeps them in place by his great power. For the reader, it means the God who runs the universe also knows and cares about the details.
entries.40:27: God challenges Israel's complaint that he doesn't see their situation or care about their rights. For the reader, it means God does see your struggle, even when it feels like he's ignoring you.
entries.40:28: The eternal God, creator of the whole earth, never grows tired or weak, and his understanding is beyond our grasp. For the reader, it means you can trust a God who never runs out of strength or wisdom.
entries.40:29: God gives strength to the tired and power to those who have none. For the reader, it means when you're exhausted, God is the one who can renew you.
entries.40:30: Even young people get tired and worn out and stumble. For the reader, it means human strength has limits, so don't be ashamed when you reach yours.
entries.40:31: Waiting on God is not doing nothing; it is drawing strength from him. That strength outlasts your own.
entries.41:1: God invites the nations to come quietly and present their case before him. It means we should stop and listen to God rather than argue with him.
entries.41:2: God asks who raised up a conqueror from the east who succeeds wherever he goes and defeats kings easily. It means God is the one who directs history and gives victory.
entries.41:3: The conqueror moves quickly and safely, as if he barely touches the ground. It means his success is swift and unstoppable because God is behind it.
entries.41:4: God says he is the one who planned all this and has been Lord from the beginning to the end. It means the same God who started history is still in charge today.
entries.41:5: The distant lands see what God is doing and are afraid, and they gather together. It means God's power makes people take notice, whether in fear or in response.
entries.41:6: People encourage one another and offer help to their neighbors. It means when people are afraid, they often turn to each other for courage instead of to God.
entries.41:7: Craftsmen encourage each other as they build an idol and nail it down so it won't fall over. It means people work hard to make something to trust in, but it is only a thing they made.
entries.41:8: God turns to Israel, calling them his servant and descendants of his friend Abraham. It means God has a special, personal relationship with his people.
entries.41:9: God says he called his people from far away and chose them, and he has not rejected them. It means God's commitment to his people does not depend on distance or circumstance.
entries.41:10: Do not panic: God is with you, will strengthen you, and will hold you up. Four promises in one sentence.
entries.41:11: God promises that everyone angry with his people will be humbled and disgraced. It means those who oppose God's people will not win in the end.
entries.41:12: God says the enemies of his people will disappear completely. It means the threats that seem so real now will one day be gone.
entries.41:13: God says he holds his people's hand and tells them not to be afraid because he will help. It means we are not alone; God himself is with us and supports us.
entries.41:14: God tells weak and helpless Jacob not to fear because he will help and defend them. It means even when we feel small and powerless, God stands up for us.
entries.41:15: God promises to make his people strong like a sharp threshing tool that crushes mountains. It means God can turn the weak into people who overcome huge obstacles.
entries.41:16: God says his people will scatter their enemies like chaff in the wind and then rejoice in him. It means victory comes from God, and it leads to joy in him.
entries.41:17: God says he hears the poor and thirsty who have no water. It means God pays attention to people in desperate need and does not abandon them.
entries.41:18: God promises to make rivers and springs appear in dry, empty places. It means God can bring life and relief where there seems to be none.
entries.41:19: God says he will plant many kinds of trees in the barren land. It means God brings growth and beauty to places that were once hopeless.
entries.41:20: God does this so people will see it, understand, and recognize that he has done it. It means God's works are meant to lead people to know him.
entries.41:21: God challenges the nations to present their case and bring their best arguments. It means God is not afraid of questions and invites honest examination.
entries.41:22: God asks the idols to tell the future or explain the past so people can evaluate them. It means false gods cannot actually predict or explain anything real.
entries.41:23: God challenges the idols to do something, good or bad, so people can see and be amazed. It means idols are powerless; they cannot act at all.
entries.41:24: God says the idols are nothing and their works are worthless, and those who trust them are foolish. It means putting your trust in anything other than God is a dead end.
entries.41:25: God says he will raise up a ruler from the north who will conquer nations like dust underfoot. It means God is the one who brings down rulers and directs their paths.
entries.41:26: God asks who foretold all this from the beginning, and says no one did. It means only God knows and declares the future; the idols have said nothing.
entries.41:27: God says he was the first to announce this good news to Zion and Jerusalem. It means God speaks first and tells his people what is coming.
entries.41:28: God looked but found no one, not even a wise person, who could answer his questions. It means human wisdom and idols have nothing to say when God speaks.
entries.41:29: God concludes that the idols are all worthless, their works are nothing, and their images are as useless as wind. It means anything we trust instead of God cannot help us at all.
entries.42:1: God points to his chosen servant, whom he holds up and delights in, and gives him his Spirit to bring true knowledge of God to all nations. For the reader, this shows God works through a humble chosen one to reach the whole world.
entries.42:2: This servant will not shout or make a big public show; he works quietly. For the reader, God's work often comes gently rather than with noise and spectacle.
entries.42:3: He is careful with people who are weak and nearly broken, like a bent reed or a dimly burning wick, and he keeps bringing God's truth to people. For the reader, God does not toss aside the fragile but treats them with care.
entries.42:4: He will not give up or be worn down until God's truth reaches the whole earth, and distant lands wait for his teaching. For the reader, this mission is certain to succeed, so hope in it is well placed.
entries.42:5: God introduces himself as the Creator who made the heavens and earth, gives its produce, and gives breath and life to everyone on it. For the reader, the one speaking has full authority over all life, including yours.
entries.42:6: God says he has called this servant, held his hand, and kept him safe, making him a covenant for the people and a light for the nations. For the reader, God's purpose is to bring light and relationship to the whole world.
entries.42:7: The servant's job is to open blind eyes and free prisoners held in dark dungeons. For the reader, God's work includes real rescue for people trapped in darkness and bondage.
entries.42:8: God declares his name is the Lord and he will not share his glory with anyone else or with idols. For the reader, God alone deserves our worship and praise.
entries.42:9: God says the earlier predictions have come true, and now he announces new things before they happen. For the reader, God can be trusted because he shows he knows and controls the future.
entries.42:10: Everyone everywhere, including those at sea and in distant lands, is called to sing a new song of praise to the Lord. For the reader, praising God is for all people, not just one group.
entries.42:11: Even the desert, its flocks, and the nomadic camps are told to rejoice and shout for joy from the mountains. For the reader, all of creation and every kind of people can join in gladness before God.
entries.42:12: The peoples of distant coastlands are to give glory to the Lord and declare his praise. For the reader, worship of God is meant to spread to the ends of the earth.
entries.42:13: God will act like a mighty warrior, raising his voice and moving with fierce energy against his enemies. For the reader, God is not passive; he is strong and will defend his cause.
entries.42:14: God says he has been silent and restrained for a long time, but now he will act with intense, painful effort like a woman in labor. For the reader, God's patience has a limit, and he will finally step in.
entries.42:15: God will lay waste mountains and hills, dry up their plants, and turn rivers and pools into dry ground. For the reader, nothing in nature can stand in the way of God's purpose.
entries.42:16: God will lead blind people along unfamiliar paths, turning darkness into light and rough ground into level road, and he will not abandon them. For the reader, God promises to guide those who cannot see their way and to stay with them.
entries.42:17: Those who trust in carved images and call metal statues their gods will be turned back and deeply shamed. For the reader, putting your ultimate hope in anything other than God ends in disappointment.
entries.42:18: God calls those who are deaf and blind to pay attention and open their eyes so they can see. For the reader, God invites people who have not been listening to wake up and understand.
entries.42:19: God asks who is blind and deaf like his own servant, the one he sends, who is supposed to be devoted to him. For the reader, even God's own people can fail to see and hear what he is doing.
entries.42:20: The servant sees a lot but remembers nothing, and has open ears but does not really hear. For the reader, it is possible to be exposed to God's truth and still not take it in.
entries.42:21: The Lord was pleased, because of his own righteousness, to make his teaching great and honored. For the reader, God's instruction is valuable and worthy of respect, not something to ignore.
entries.42:22: But the people have been plundered and trapped in prisons and holes, with no one to rescue them or demand them back. For the reader, ignoring God leads to real loss and captivity.
entries.42:23: God asks who among the people will listen to this and pay attention for the future. For the reader, the question is whether you will take God's warning seriously now.
entries.42:24: God himself handed Jacob and Israel over to plunderers because they sinned against him and refused to follow his teaching. For the reader, the troubles that come from rejecting God are not accidents but consequences.
entries.42:25: God poured out his fierce anger like fire all around them, but they did not notice or take it to heart. For the reader, it is dangerous to go through hardship and never stop to learn from it.
entries.43:1: God tells his people not to be afraid because he made them and claims them as his own, calling each by name. You can face fear knowing you belong to the one who made you and stands up for you.
entries.43:2: The water and the fire are not removed, but you do not go through them alone. His presence is the protection.
entries.43:3: God reminds Israel that he is their God and rescuer, and he was willing to give other nations in exchange for them. Your safety and rescue matter to God, and he acts on your behalf.
entries.43:4: God says his people are precious and honored in his eyes, and he loves them, so he gives others in exchange for their lives. You are deeply valued and loved by God, not because of what you do.
entries.43:5: God tells them not to fear because he is with them, and he will gather their scattered children from east and west. Even when you feel scattered or far away, God is with you and brings you back.
entries.43:6: God commands the north and south to release his people, bringing his sons and daughters home from far away. God actively works to bring his scattered children back to himself.
entries.43:7: Everyone who bears God's name was made by him and formed for his glory. Your life has purpose because you were made by God and for his glory.
entries.43:8: God calls forward a people who have eyes and ears but cannot see or hear. People can be close to God yet still miss what he is doing, so we need him to open our eyes.
entries.43:9: God challenges the nations to prove their idols can explain the past or predict the future, and to bring witnesses who confirm it. Only God can truly explain history and back up his claims.
entries.43:10: God says his people are his witnesses and chosen servant, so they may know and believe him, since there was no God before him and none after. You are called to know and trust God and to show others who he is.
entries.43:11: God declares that he alone is the Lord and there is no savior besides him. No one else can rescue you the way God can.
entries.43:12: God says he announced and saved and made things clear, with no foreign god among them, so they are his witnesses. God has shown himself faithful, and his people can testify to what he has done.
